Despite the growing use of digital health strategies in stroke management, evidence supporting seamless and timely care coordination from the emergency medical services (EMS) to the emergency department (ED) remains limited. Brain Saver, a newly developed mobile app, addresses this gap by facilitating real-time data sharing between EMS personnel and ED clinicians during stroke transport.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: This study aimed to examine the potential of the Brain Saver protocol to improve existing EMS-ED workflows in emergency stroke transport by describing its functional components, implementing a pilot intervention in a real-world setting, and exploring its preliminary impact on treatment timeliness.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Data were collected in Pohang, South Korea, from December 2023 to April 2024 through collaboration with 2 fire stations, eight 119 EMS and safety centers, 3 hospitals, and SEERS Technology. Preintervention training and postintervention surveys were conducted among EMS personnel (n=80) and clinicians (n=24). In this pilot, patients with stroke (ICD-10 [International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision] codes I60-I63) in the intervention group (n=34) were transported using ambulances equipped with the Brain Saver mobile app, while the comparison group (n=129) was transported by standard ambulances to the same hospitals during the study period. With "needle" defined as any parenteral treatment, onset-to-door time and door-to-needle time were compared by group. After exact matching on age, baseline stroke severity, stroke type, and destination hospital, intervention effects were estimated using generalized estimating equations.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Participants (N=163) had a mean age of 69.4 (SD 15.2) years, 50.3% (82/163) were male, and 65.6% (107/163) had ischemic stroke. No significant baseline differences, including stroke severity, were observed between groups. The median onset-to-needle time was shorter in the intervention group than in the comparison group (114 vs 204 minutes; P=.03). In the matched analytic sample (n=91), the intervention group showed significant reductions in onset-to-needle time (Exp(β)=0.49; P=.009) and door-to-needle time (Exp(β)=0.67; P=.04) compared with the comparison group.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Integrating digital health into emergency stroke transport may improve care timeliness by supporting real-time prehospital notification and facilitating prompt in-hospital responses. The Brain Saver mobile app shows potential use for reducing onset-to-treatment time. Further larger-scale studies are needed to evaluate implementation fidelity and scalability.

articles.title: There are No Differences in Early Complications or One-Year Patient Reported Outcomes Between Single-Stage Bilateral and Unilateral Total Hip Arthroplasty Performed in Patients 70 Years and Older.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Despite the potential benefits of single-stage bilateral total hip arthroplasty (ssBTHA), its safety in older patients remains unclear. This study compared early postoperative complications and patient reported outcomes (PROs) between patients 70 years and older undergoing ssBTHA and similar-aged patients undergoing unilateral total hip arthroplasty (UTHA).

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Data were collected retrospectively for 334 patients 70 and older who underwent UTHA (271 patients) or ssBTHA (63 patients) by a single, high-volume arthroplasty surgeon between July 2017 and July 2022. Patient demographics, perioperative variables, early postoperative complications (within 90 days), and PROs up to one year were collected. Patient demographics were comparable between cohorts, except for the proportion of women, which was higher in the ssBTHA cohort (P = 0.043). Continuous variables were compared using t-tests and categorical variables using chi-square or Fisher's exact tests.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: The ssBTHA cohort had a longer length of stay (P < 0.001), a lower proportion of patients discharged directly home (P < 0.001), and higher postoperative transfusion rates (P = 0.005) compared with the UTHA cohort. There were no statistically significant differences in 90-day emergency department visits, readmissions from the emergency department, venous thromboembolisms, nonrevision reoperations, or revisions between cohorts. There were no differences in preoperative or postoperative PROs observed through one year postsurgery.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: A ssBTHA is a reasonable and safe treatment option for patients 70 years of age and older who have symptomatic bilateral hip osteoarthritis, with early postoperative complication profiles and PROs comparable to those of unilateral procedures.

articles.title: Echocardiographic changes in hyperthyroid cats: Comparison of subclinical disease and congestive heart failure.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Hyperthyroidism induces a wide spectrum of cardiovascular changes in cats, yet the factors distinguishing subclinical cardiac involvement from congestive heart failure (CHF) remain poorly defined. Previous studies have focused primarily on structural changes, with limited evaluation of atrial function or right-sided involvement.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: To compare echocardiographic variables between hyperthyroid cats with subclinical cardiac disease and those presenting in CHF, with emphasis on left atrial remodelling, left atrial function, and left ventricular dimensional changes, and right-sided involvement assessed by right atrial diameter. The comparison of clinical and biochemical variables was a secondary objective.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A retrospective case-control study was performed using medical records of 51 hyperthyroid cats with subclinical cardiac disease and 47 hyperthyroid cats presenting in CHF. All cats underwent standard echocardiography, serum biochemistry including total thyroxine (TT4). Type of congestion was determined by thoracic radiography or point-of-care ultrasound, and CHF cats were classified as having pulmonary oedema only or pleural/mixed effusion.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Cats with CHF had significantly larger atrial dimensions and increased left ventricular internal diameter compared with subclinical cats. Left atrial dysfunction was the most robust discriminator between groups. Pleural or mixed effusion was the predominant CHF phenotype and, compared with pulmonary oedema alone, was associated with greater right-sided and global volume overload. TT4 concentrations did not differ significantly between cats with and without CHF. Similarly, biochemical variables showed no significant differences between subclinical or CHF cats or between CHF subtypes.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Atrial remodelling - particularly impaired atrial function and biatrial enlargement - represents the clearest echocardiographic marker of decompensation in hyperthyroid cats. The predominance of pleural or mixed effusion highlights the importance of assessing right-sided cardiac measurements. Comprehensive echocardiographic evaluation is essential for early identification of cats at risk of CHF, whereas TT4 concentration alone does not predict cardiac status.

articles.title: Outcomes following impedance threshold device use during out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Existing work is equivocal regarding the benefit of impedance threshold device (ITD) use among patients experiencing out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA). We examined the association of ITD use with prehospital outcomes and longer-term dispositions in a nationally representative sample of OHCA patients.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We included adult, non-traumatic, OHCA scene runs from the 2024 ESO Data Collaborative. We compared patients treated with (a) ITD only; (b) ITD and active compression-decompression device (ITD + ACD); and (c) neither device (no ITD). Prehospital outcomes included return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) and survival to hospital arrival (SHA); disposition outcomes included survival to hospital discharge and favorable neurologic outcome (i.e., discharge to home). We used multivariate logistic regression to examine the association of treatment group with outcomes, adjusting for demographics and several potential confounders.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: We included 97,439 patient records (85.3% no ITD; 13.1% ITD only; 1.6% ITD + ACD). Disposition outcomes were available for 13,026 patients (13.4%). ROSC was higher for patients treated with ITD only (26.7%) than those treated with no ITD (23.8%; aOR = 1.09 [1.04, 1.14]); a similar pattern emerged for SHA. Conversely, survival to discharge was lower for patients treated with ITD only (23.9%) than those treated with no ITD (32.0%; aOR = 0.68, [0.61, 0.76]); a similar pattern emerged for favorable neurologic outcome. The ITD + ACD group showed more extreme versions of the trends observed for ITD only.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: ITD use was associated with improved prehospital outcomes but worsened dispositional outcomes among patients experiencing OHCA, suggesting this device may prove beneficial early in resuscitation of OHCA patients.

articles.title: Determinants of unwitnessed out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: a systematic review (HL-D-26-00618).
articles.journal_full: Heart & lung : the journal of critical care

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Approximately half of all out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) cases are unwitnessed, with survival rates below 5%. Although early recognition is critical for improving outcomes, factors associated with unwitnessed OHCA have not been systematically reviewed.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: To systematically review and synthesize the available evidence on determinants of unwitnessed OHCA.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We included peer-reviewed observational studies investigating associations between demographic, socioeconomic, clinical, or situational factors and witnessed status of OHCA in adults. No restrictions were placed on setting, language, or publication year. A systematic search of MEDLINE, Embase, and Web of Science Core Collection was performed from inception to July 17, 2025. Risk of bias was assessed using the QUIPS tool. Findings were synthesized narratively by determinant domain, summarizing study counts, effect directions, statistical significance, and consistency.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Twenty-two studies including 210,028 individuals were analyzed. Female sex and arrest occurring at home were most consistently associated with unwitnessed OHCA. Limited evidence, predominantly from unadjusted analyses, suggested higher rates of unwitnessed OHCA among Black individuals, those with low socioeconomic status or living in more deprived areas, individuals with type I diabetes, psychiatric illness, and arrests occurring at night, during sleep, or in residential or rural settings.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: This systematic review identified several factors associated with unwitnessed OHCA, with the most consistent evidence for female sex and arrests occurring at home. These findings may help guide targeted prevention and public health strategies.

articles.title: Acute Imbalance Syndrome vs Acute Vestibular Syndrome: Clinical and Topographical Differentiation.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: Stroke is a major differential diagnosis in patients with acute vertigo/dizziness or imbalance. Current diagnostic algorithms such as head impulse test, gaze-evoked nystagmus, and test of skew are optimized for presentations with spontaneous nystagmus (SPN), traditionally called acute vestibular syndrome (AVS). However, in recent studies, a relevant proportion of patients with stroke-related vertigo/dizziness had no SPN, but rather postural or gait imbalance, a phenotype lately termed acute imbalance syndrome (AIS). We aimed to outline the pathoanatomical differences of stroke-related AIS vs AVS and its clinical implications.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Patients with MRI-proven stroke-related acute vertigo/dizziness or imbalance were included in this emergency department (ED) cohort study at LMU Hospital prospectively. Vestibular, ocular motor, and postural signs were documented (including SPN presence/intensity by video oculography, postural imbalance by posturography). Patients were classified as suffering from AIS or AVS based on the presence of SPN. Stroke lesion distribution was depicted in Montreal Neurological Institute space and supplemented by structural disconnectome mapping from the lesion cores. Multivariate lesion symptom-mapping based on support-vector regression and disconnectome mapping was applied for SPN intensity and sway path as surrogate markers for AVS and AIS.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Of 75 patients (age: 65.7 ± 13.3 years, 40% female), 58.7% were diagnosed with AIS, 38.7% with AVS, and 2.7% with central positional vertigo. In AIS, the lesion core was located in the anterior cerebellar lobe and deep cerebellar nuclei (superior cerebellar artery/posterior inferior cerebellar artery territory) connecting to the bilateral pontomesencephalic tegmentum through the superior cerebellar peduncle. AVS stroke lesions were mostly located in the posterior cerebellar/flocculonodular lobe (posterior inferior cerebellar artery/anterior inferior cerebellar artery territory) and connected to the ipsilesional vestibular nucleus (VN) and bilateral medial longitudinal fascicle (MLF) through the inferior cerebellar peduncle. SPN intensity correlated with voxels in the cerebellar lobules VI-IX connecting to VN and MLF. Postural sway was associated with a small local cluster in the cerebellar Crus I.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: AIS accounts for more than half of patients with stroke-related vertigo/dizziness or imbalance. AIS lesions were located in the anterior cerebellar lobe, disturbing cerebellar-pontomesencephalic networks for posture and gait control. AVS lesions affected the posterior cerebellar/flocculonodular lobe and associated vestibulo-ocular reflex networks. Recognition of both clinical phenotypes is essential to identify all strokes among patients with vertigo/dizziness in the emergency setting.

articles.title: Emergency Department Visits for Falls and First-Time Seizure.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: Unrecognized seizures occur in up to 77% of individuals with epilepsy, leading to delays in diagnosis with significant consequences including injury, mortality, impaired psychosocial functioning, and negative socioeconomic impacts. Falls are a common reason to present to the emergency department (ED) and may be a sentinel sign of an unrecognized seizure. Whether falls represent missed opportunities for earlier seizure recognition remains unknown. We therefore evaluated the temporal association between ED visits for falls and first-time seizure.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted a retrospective case-crossover study using the State Inpatient Databases and State Emergency Department Databases from 11 states (Arkansas, Florida, Georgia, Iowa, Massachusetts, Maryland, Nebraska, New York, Utah, Vermont, and Wisconsin) between 2016 and 2021. Adults aged 18 years and older with an acute care visit for a first-time seizure were identified using ICD-10 codes. Using patients as their own controls, we applied conditional logistic regression to compare the odds of an ED visit for a fall during prespecified case periods preceding the seizure (1-7, 8-30, 31-90, and 91-180 days prior) vs corresponding control periods 1 year earlier. Prespecified intervals were selected to assess graded temporal proximity.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: There were 57,547 patients with a first-time seizure and 7,307 patients (mean age 49.3 years and 55.2% female) with at least one prior ED visit for a fall during the case or control periods. ED visits for a fall were more common in case compared with control periods, with the highest odds in the 7 days immediately before the acute care visit for first-time seizure (OR = 2.6, 95% CI 2.2-3.2). In a week-by-week analysis, the association persisted up to 22 weeks before seizure, demonstrating temporal attenuation as time from the event increased. These findings were consistent across age and sex strata and after excluding those who had traumatic brain injury. In analyses restricted to first-time status epilepticus, the association in the 7 days preceding seizure was most pronounced (OR = 4.5, 95% CI 2.5-9.0).

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: ED visits for falls are more common immediately preceding first-time seizure, potentially representing missed opportunities for earlier diagnosis, evaluation, and intervention. Prospective studies are needed to clarify the underlying mechanisms and clinical implications.

articles.title: Development of a protocol to retrospectively identify acute traumatic brain injury using electronic medical records from an academic health system data warehouse.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: As recommended in the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke TBI Classification and Nomenclature Initiative, retrospective identification of traumatic brain injury (TBI) from electronic medical record (EMR) data offers major potential for research and surveillance. Enterprise data warehouses integrating structured and unstructured EMR data could support this work, yet few studies have evaluated their use for TBI case ascertainment. This study describes a manual chart review protocol to identify acute TBI among patients receiving head CT scan from a large health system's enterprise data warehouse.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We identified encounters potentially related to TBI using clinical documentation files (e.g., Emergency Department Triage, History & Physical, Discharge Summary) within our institution's enterprise data warehouse. Two independent raters applied the protocol to 126 patients who presented in 2019 and underwent head computed tomography (CT). Sampling was limited to patients receiving a head CT scan to enrich the cohort with both TBI and non‑TBI cases. We developed a decision tree workflow to guide documentation of a plausible mechanism of head injury accompanied by clinical symptoms and/or clinically indicated neuroimaging. Criteria were adapted from the American Congress of Rehabilitation Medicine definition of mild TBI and modified for retrospective EMR data. Raters classified each case as (1) no evidence of acute TBI, (2) sufficient evidence of acute TBI, or (3) inconclusive evidence due to missing data or confounding conditions (e.g., syncope).

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Inter‑rater reliability demonstrated strong agreement across raters (88.1% agreement; Cohen's κ = 0.80 (95% CI: 0.71-0.89), p < 0.0001); inter-rater reliability was similar across subgroups of age (± 65 years), sex, and payor (government/non-government insurance). Among the 126 cases reviewed, there was agreement on sufficient evidence of acute TBI for 49 cases (86.0% agreement between rater 1 and 2), no evidence of acute TBI for 54 cases (96.4% agreement), and inconclusive evidence for 8 cases (61.5% agreement). Sensitivity analyses reweighting the sample to parent cohort marginal distributions produced similar results (94.2% agreement, κ = 0.74 (95% CI: 0.58-0.90).

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: This manual chart review protocol showed strong inter‑rater reliability for identifying acute TBI using EMR data. Future research should examine external reliability in other health systems and compare its performance with International Classification of Diseases‑based definitions and prospective diagnosis. As enterprise data warehouses become more ubiquitous, reliable case ascertainment protocols such as this could facilitate standardized, scalable retrospective identification of TBI, supporting retrospective TBI cohort studies.

articles.title: Hospital-wide interventions to reduce emergency department overcrowding: Data-driven strategies and clinical governance at an Italian teaching hospital.

abstract.text: BackgroundEmergency Department (ED) overcrowding is a global systemic challenge driven by an imbalance between healthcare demand and resource availability. This study evaluates a multifaceted, organization-wide intervention at an Italian teaching hospital by focusing on throughput and output factors.MethodsA quasi-experimental, pre-post design analysed 100% of the available population data (N = 199354 visits) from 2019 to 2024. A "Digital Twin" simulation identified boarding as the primary bottleneck, consuming 47% of medical resources. Interventions included a "Discharge Decalogue," digitalization of community care pathways (ADI/CAVS), and nursing protocols. Statistical significance for patient satisfaction (N = 1840) was assessed via t-tests (95% CI).ResultsDespite a 23.6% increase in total ED volume and a 37.8% surge in high-complexity presentations (Red Codes), interventions optimized outflow. The ALOS for complex discharges decreased for both CAVS (-24.6%) and ADI (-22.6%). Throughput protocols reduced chest pain response times by 27.7%. Satisfaction scores improved accordingly, particularly within the information domain (p < 0.001; 95/% CI [0.22, 0.38]). While overall waiting times fell by 17.8%, boarding times increased: this was driven by clinical complexity and a deliberate institutional policy to mitigate medical boarding within surgical units. This strategic prioritization was maintained to preserve elective surgical capacity.ConclusionsA systems-based approach prioritizing output optimization and hospital-territory integration demonstrates superior efficacy compared to traditional input-reduction strategies. This data-driven model provides a scalable framework to strengthen clinical governance and enhance patient experience within resource-constrained environments.

articles.title: Field-Based Assessment of Running Biomechanics Using Global Positioning System/Inertial Measurement Unit: Establishing Construct Validity in Elite Athletes.
articles.journal_full: Journal of strength and conditioning research

abstract.text: Weber, JA, Peeling, P, Hart, NH, and Newton, RU. Field-based assessment of running biomechanics using global positioning system/inertial measurement unit: Establishing construct validity in elite athletes. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-To examine the between-session reliability and construct validity of global positioning system (GPS)/inertial measurement unit (IMU)-derived biomechanical variables during field-based running in elite athletes. Fifty-four professional male Australian Football League players completed repeated 40-m runs across 1 competitive season (3,943 trials). Running speed for the 20-40 m segment was quantified via 10-Hz GPS and center-of-mass displacement metrics derived from a 100-Hz IMU. Between-session reliability (n = 25, mean (k) = 2.95) was assessed using a linear mixed-effects model with velocity as a fixed covariate, expressed as intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) (absolute agreement), SEM, and minimal detectable change95, with 95% confidence intervals from athlete-cluster bootstrap. Five candidate models were compared; Multivariate Adaptive Regression Splines was selected based on lowest cross-validation root mean squared error (RMSE). Validity was assessed over 100 iterations of athlete-stratified cross-validation (80/20 split), with agreement quantified by ICC, RMSE, and athlete-level Bland-Altman analysis. Velocity-adjusted reliability ranged from moderate to good-to-excellent across 12 variables (ICC = 0.65-0.92), with 8 meeting good-to-excellent thresholds (ICC ≥0.75). Multivariate Adaptive Regression Splines accounted for 93% of variance in running speed (R2 = 0.93; RMSE = 0.20 m·s-1; ICC = 0.96 ± 0.004). Athlete-level Bland-Altman analysis indicated negligible bias (-0.01 m·s-1; LoA: -0.243 to +0.223 m·s-1) with no proportional bias (p = 0.369); limits narrowed in athletes with adequate data volume (n = 47; -0.207 to +0.189 m·s-1). Mechanics-speed relationships persisted after accounting for within-athlete clustering (residual between-athlete ICC = 0.43), and the most influential predictors were consistent with established biomechanical determinants of speed. These findings support GPS/IMU-derived biomechanical variables as field-based indicators of running mechanics. Pending replication and criterion validation, this approach may offer practitioners an accessible framework for monitoring performance and rehabilitation.

articles.title: Comment on: "over-the-counter drug poisoning among pediatric and adolescent patients presenting to emergency departments: a nationwide analysis of the COVID-19 impact".
Knowledge and Anxiety Levels of Parents of Children Admitted to the Emergency Department due to Intoxication.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: This descriptive and correlational study aimed to determine the knowledge and anxiety levels of parents of children who presented to the emergency department due to intoxication.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: The study was conducted between January 2024 and April 2025 with the parents of 96 children aged 1-6 years who were brought to the pediatric emergency department of a university hospital in Konya, Turkey, due to intoxication. Data were collected using a Sociodemographic Information Form for Parents and Children, an Intoxication Information Form, and the State Anxiety Inventory. Ethical committee approval, institutional permission, and informed consent from the parents were obtained. Data were analyzed using IBM SPSS 26 statistical software, employing frequency, percentage, mean, standard deviation, median, minimum and maximum values, Cronbach's alpha, t test, analysis of variance, Bonferroni, Pearson correlation, and regression analysis. A P value < .05 was considered statistically significant.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: It was determined that 63.5% of the parents participating in the study were mothers, and 59.4% were under 35 years of age. Additionally, 8.3% of the children had a prior history of poisoning, 66.7% were between 1-3 years old, 54.2% were brought to the hospital within the first 30 minutes, and 66.7% were poisoned because of drugs. Parents' knowledge of intoxication was found to be at a moderate level, with a score of 18.65 (2.92), and their situational anxiety was at a mild level, with a score of 49.54 (12.42). The study found that parents over 35 years of age, parents with a primary/secondary school education, and parents living in towns/villages had higher levels of knowledge about intoxication than others. Anxiety levels were found to be higher in mothers than in fathers and in parents over 35 than in those under 35 (P < .05). A significant negative correlation was found between parents' knowledge of intoxication and their situational anxiety scores (r = -0.411; P < .05).

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: The study concluded that as parents' knowledge of intoxication increases, their situational anxiety levels decrease. Based on these results, it is recommended that parents be informed about intoxication and be included in educational programs for preschool groups.

articles.title: Life-course hygiene exposures and disorders of gut-brain interaction: a multinational cross-sectional study.

abstract.text: Despite growing interest in its role in immune-mediated diseases, the relevance of the hygiene hypothesis to disorders of gut-brain interaction (DGBI) remains unclear. We aimed to examine the associations between childhood and adulthood hygiene-related exposures and DGBI prevalence, and to assess whether these associations persist after adjustment for sociodemographic and national development indicators. This cross-sectional study included 54,127 adults from 26 countries. DGBI were defined using Rome IV criteria. Childhood (≤ 7 years) and adulthood hygiene-related exposures included farm residence and access to running water, electricity, and rural residence. Country-level development was assessed using the Human Development Index (HDI). After adjustment for sociodemographic factors and psychological distress, several individual exposures showed independent associations with DGBI. Childhood farm exposure was independently associated with higher odds of DGBI (OR=1.11, 95% CI 1.03-1.19), irritable bowel syndrome (OR=1.21, 95% CI 1.03-1.42), and functional dyspepsia (OR=1.22, 95% CI 1.08-1.38). In contrast, rural residence (OR=0.88, 95% CI 0.82-0.95) and absence of running water (OR=0.83, 95% CI 0.77-0.90) or electricity (OR=0.86, 95% CI 0.77-0.97) in adulthood were associated with lower odds of DGBI. These associations remained statistically significant after additional adjustment for HDI. Several individual hygiene-related environmental exposures were associated with DGBI, suggesting that environmental conditions may be associated with global variation in DGBI burden.

articles.title: Respiratory function, functional capacity, dyspnea, and sleep quality in young adults using the IQOS heated tobacco product: a matched cross-sectional study.

abstract.text: This matched cross-sectional study compared respiratory function, respiratory muscle strength, functional exercise capacity, dyspnea, and sleep quality between young IQOS users and matched control subjects. This study involved 31 young adult IQOS users and 31 age/sex/body mass index-matched never-tobacco users who underwent a standardized testing protocol during a single visit. Spirometry, maximal inspiratory pressure (MIP), 6-min walk test (6MWT), modified Medical Research Council (mMRC) dyspnea scale, modified Borg Scale (mBorg), and Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) scores were compared. While mean resting lung functions were similar between groups (all p > 0.05), IQOS users had shorter 6MWT distances (591.1 [580.2 - 638.4] meters vs. 626.0 [600.5 - 683.8] meters, p = 0.003, r = 0.53) and higher mMRC dyspnea scores (median mMRC Grade = 1 (0-1) in IQOS users vs 0 (0-0) in controls, p < 0.001, r = 0.62), higher mBorg dyspnea scores at the end of the 6MWT (median end-6MWT mBorg rating scale 1 [0-2] vs 0 [0-1], p = 0.001, r = 0.57), and poor sleep quality (PSQI global score 6.32 ± 2.63 vs 4.58 ± 1.61, p = 0.012, r = 0.45). Additionally, while MIP values tended toward being lower in IQOS users, these differences were statistically nonsignificant (p = 0.090). In conclusion, young exclusive IQOS users showed lower functional exercise capacity, greater dyspnea, and poorer sleep quality than matched never-users despite comparable resting spirometry, and these hypothesis-generating findings warrant longitudinal evaluation with biochemical exposure verification.

articles.title: Assessing health advocacy competencies through a novel simulation OSCE-based educational framework.

abstract.text: Health advocacy remains one of the least explicitly assessed CanMEDS roles in Emergency Medicine. Objective structured clinical examination (OSCE) simulation is used to assess performance in real time but has not previously incorporated social determinants of health. We developed and piloted a simulation-based OSCE, embedding advocacy within acute clinical care and introduced novel assessment tools, completed by both examiners and standardized patients. Here we report the feasibility and acceptability of this OSCE and assessment tools. Twenty-two residents completed the advocacy and standard cases; 18 (82%) completed exit surveys. Most participants did not know advocacy would be assessed. Participants described the case as realistic and acceptable with minor suggestions for refinement. Assessors found the assessments intuitive to use and feasible to implement. This pilot suggests structured assessment of patient-level advocacy from both physician and patient perspectives can be feasibly integrated into simulation assessment without disrupting usual performance evaluation.

articles.title: Performance of updated American College of Surgeons field triage guidelines in identifying need for trauma center care.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: The Guidelines for the Field Triage of injured patients were updated in 2021 to improve the reliability of prehospital trauma triage. The objective of this study was to describe the association of the 2021 Field Triage Guidelines criteria with need for advanced trauma center care from a cohort of patients transported to a level 1 trauma center.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This was a health records review of Field Triage Guidelines criteria met for trauma team activations at a level 1 trauma center from January 2020 to December 2021. Hospital-based and injury severity score (ISS)-based trauma center need were defined and sensitivity and specificity of the Field Triage Guidelines calculated for both. Area under the receiver operator curves were used to assess accuracy. Multivariable logistic regression was used to evaluate the association of each criterion with trauma center need.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 1427 patients were included and 90.3% met at least one Field Triage Guidelines criteria. Overall, patients meeting hospital-based trauma center need was 33.8% compared to 28.4% which met ISS-based trauma center need. Field Triage Guidelines criteria demonstrated a sensitivity of 97.3% and specificity of 13.3% with respect to hospital-based trauma center need with an area under the ROC of 0.80. Mental status and vital signs showed the highest association with trauma center need.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: The updated 2021 Field Triage Guidelines demonstrate good accuracy when assessed retrospectively on a cohort of patients transferred to a level 1 trauma center. The very high sensitivity of the new guidelines may help to reduce undertriage rates to the international goal of <5%. New criteria in this iteration of the Field Triage Guidelines could lead to improved rates of undertriage specifically in severely injured geriatric patients.

articles.title: Submandibular-window point-of-care ultrasound as a bedside clue to deep extension of a peritonsillar abscess.
Surgeon-perceived intraoperative complexity is associated with early adverse outcomes after major emergency abdominal surgery: a prospective cohort study.
articles.journal_full: European journal of trauma and emergency surgery : official publication of the European Trauma Society

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Intraoperative complexity in major emergency abdominal surgery lacks a standardized definition and is rarely quantified prospectively. Whether surgeon-perceived intraoperative complexity is associated with short-term postoperative outcomes remains unknown.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: In this single-center prospective cohort study, 411 patients undergoing major emergency abdominal surgery were included. Immediately after surgery, the operating surgeon rated perceived intraoperative complexity on a 0-10 scale. The association between surgeon-perceived intraoperative complexity and the primary outcome, 30-day unplanned reoperation, was investigated using Fine-Gray regression. The model was adjusted for age, sex, body mass index, performance status, and intraoperative pathology. Secondary outcomes were 30-day mortality, length of stay, and Comprehensive Complication Index.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Unplanned reoperation occurred in 15% and 30-day mortality in 11%. Higher surgeon-perceived intraoperative complexity was associated with reoperation (sHR 1.20 per point; 95% CI 1.08-1.34). Complexity was also associated with prolonged LOS (β 1.47 days per unit increase; 95% CI 0.93-2.01), higher CCI category (OR 1.24 per unit increase; 95% CI 1.14-1.35), and increased 30-day mortality (OR 1.25; 95% CI 1.07-1.45).

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Surgeon-perceived intraoperative complexity was associated with reoperation, morbidity, and 30-day mortality after major emergency abdominal surgery. These findings suggest that the operating surgeon's assessment may capture clinically meaningful prognostic information beyond conventional baseline risk factors. External validation and evaluation of inter-rater reproducibility are needed before clinical implementation.

articles.title: Finnish Paramedics' Self-Assessed Competence in Paediatric and Neonatal Care: A Nationwide Survey of Education, Training and Development Needs.

abstract.label: AIM
abstract.text: To explore Finnish paramedics' self-assessed competence in paediatric and neonatal care and identify educational and training needs.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This cross-sectional survey included 253 graduates of Finnish bachelor-level paramedic programmes. Data were collected between January and March 2026 using a Webropol questionnaire distributed through social media. The survey assessed self-perceived competence in paediatric and neonatal care, educational experiences, training opportunities and development needs. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics, composite variables and non-parametric methods.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Participants reported moderate competence in paediatric care (mean 2.92) and lower competence in neonatal care (mean 2.04). Younger and less experienced paramedics reported higher competence in theoretical and assessment-related domains, whereas more experienced paramedics reported stronger competence in emergency response performance and stress management. Competence in paediatric mental and behavioural health emergencies was consistently rated lowest (mean 1.30). Neonatal assessment and resuscitation skills also received relatively low ratings. Participants reported limited opportunities for simulation-based training and clinical placements, particularly in neonatal care.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Paramedics identified important competence gaps in paediatric and neonatal care, especially in mental health emergencies and neonatal practice. Strengthening undergraduate education, simulation-based learning and continuing professional development may improve preparedness for paediatric and neonatal emergencies.

articles.title: Faecal urgency in Crohn's disease: associations with disease location and activity, psychobiological burden and adverse outcomes.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Faecal urgency (FU) is a frequent and disabling symptom in inflammatory bowel disease, although evidence in Crohn's disease (CD) remains limited. We aimed to evaluate the prevalence and severity of FU in CD and assess its association with disease location, inflammatory activity, psychobiological factors, quality of life (QoL), work productivity, and adverse clinical outcomes after 52 weeks.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted a single-centre observational study including adult patients with CD recruited between July-September 2024. Participants completed the Faecal Urgency Numeric Rating Scale (FU NRS), WPAI-GH, SIBDQ, and HADS questionnaires. Disease activity was assessed clinically, biochemically, endoscopically, and ultrasonographically. Patients were followed for 52 weeks for emergency room (ER) admissions, hospitalization, corticosteroid requirement, treatment escalation, surgery, and death.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 158 patients were included, of whom 109 (69.0%) reported clinically relevant FU (FU NRS ≥2). In the primary analysis, neither distal disease nor rectal involvement were significantly associated with clinically relevant FU (p=0.46 and 0.83, respectively). FU severity was not significantly correlated with inflammatory measures. Conversely, FU severity correlated with anxiety, depressive symptoms, impaired work productivity, and poorer QoL (all p<0.001). In multivariate models, FU was associated with overall work productivity loss and reduced SIBDQ scores. In an exploratory analysis, greater FU severity was associated with higher odds of ER admissions after 52 weeks (p=0.007).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: In this CD cohort, FU was significantly associated with psychobiological burden, impaired QoL, and healthcare utilization, supporting the multifactorial nature of this symptom.

articles.title: Exogenous ketosis in breath-hold diving: Promise, paradox and physiological risk.

abstract.text: Exogenous ketosis induced by ketone ester (KE) ingestion has attracted growing interest as a potential strategy to enhance physiological tolerance to reduced O2 availability. Reported benefits arise largely from KE-induced hyperventilation, which can improve systemic and tissue oxygenation during altitude exposure and hypoxic exercise, potentially complemented by favourable effects on cellular bioenergetics. Whether these responses translate to breath-hold diving, however, remains unknown. Breath-hold performance is constrained by the integrated effects of progressive hypoxaemia, CO2 accumulation, acid-base disturbance, altered cerebrovascular regulation and chemoreflex-mediated respiratory drive. Because ventilation ceases during apnoea, interventions that alter pre-apnoeic acid-base status or CO2 signalling might modify the chemical, neural and perceptual stimuli underlying the urge to breathe without slowing O2 depletion. Safety therefore depends not only on preserving cerebral O2 delivery, but also on maintaining the chemoreflex and perceptual warning signals that ordinarily precede hypoxic loss of consciousness. This review evaluates whether the established physiological effects of KE are mechanistically compatible with the unique demands of apnoea, focusing on acid-base regulation, CO2-dependent cerebrovascular control, autonomic integration and training-related adaptations in elite freedivers, including reduced chemoreflex sensitivity and enhanced cortical control of respiratory drive. We propose that benefits observed during maintained ventilation might not translate to breath-hold diving and could create a mechanistic mismatch with uncertain consequences for performance and safety. Direct apnoea-specific studies are required to determine whether KE supplementation is beneficial, neutral or harmful.

articles.title: Diagnostic Performance of the Infrascanner 2000™ for Detecting Intracranial Hemorrhage in Traumatic Brain Injury Patients in Pakistan.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: Intracranial hemorrhage (ICH) is a major cause of morbidity and mortality after traumatic brain injury (TBI). Computed tomography (CT) is often unavailable in low-resource settings, delaying diagnosis. The Infrascanner 2000™, a handheld near-infrared device, has been proposed as a rapid, noninvasive ICH screening tool. The objective of this study was to determine the diagnostic accuracy of the Infrascanner 2000™ for detecting ICH in TBI patients, compared with noncontrast CT, at 2 tertiary care hospitals in Peshawar, Pakistan.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: In this prospective observational study, 141 patients with mild, moderate, or severe TBI presenting to the emergency department of Neurosurgery at Northwest General Hospital and Lady Reading Hospital, Peshawar, Pakistan, underwent Infrascanner examination (inter-rater kappa 0.82), followed by noncontrast CT as the reference standard. Sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, likelihood ratios, balanced accuracy, and overall accuracy were calculated. Balanced accuracy (mean of sensitivity and specificity) replaced area under the curve, as the device yields a single binary operating point. Results followed Standard for Reporting Diagnostic Accuracy Studies guidelines.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: CT confirmed hemorrhage in 125 of 141 patients (88.6%). The Infrascanner showed sensitivity of 91.2%, specificity of 50.0%, positive predictive value of 93.4%, negative predictive value of 42.1%, and overall accuracy of 86.5% (positive likelihood ratio 1.82; negative likelihood ratio 0.18). Balanced accuracy was 0.706 (95% CI: 0.626-0.786), a single operating point rather than a conventional receiver operating characteristic-derived area under the curve. True positives were predominantly superficial hematomas; false negatives may reflect small or deep lesions. False positives could reflect extracranial soft-tissue injury, though this was not formally graded.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: The Infrascanner showed good sensitivity but modest specificity for ICH detection in this two-center Pakistani cohort, consistent with published series. It may serve as a rapid triage adjunct where CT access is delayed but should not replace CT imaging. Further multicenter studies, including prehospital settings, are warranted.

articles.title: Nurses' experiences with pain and fear among preschool children admitted to the emergency department.
articles.journal_full: Journal of child health care : for professionals working with children in the hospital and community

abstract.text: This study explores nurses' experiences caring for acutely ill children aged 4 to 7 years in emergency departments in Denmark in June 2023. Using a descriptive study design, semi-structured interviews were conducted with 16 nurses whose work experience ranged from 1 to 42 years. Thematic analysis identified four themes: Enhancing the nurse-child relationship, Pain and fear in pediatric emergency care, The nurse, child, and parent collaboration, and Time and workflow. Strong nurse-child relationships were found to support better care, while nurses described navigating complex, often intertwined presentations of pain and fear, requiring tailored strategies. Collaboration between nurse, child, and parent emerged as essential to creating a supportive environment, and nurses described a continual need to balance time and workflow pressures against relational, quality care. Findings suggest nurses draw on varied relational tools to engage children and parents in alleviating pain and fear, highlighting opportunities to improve pain and fear management and to more deliberately involve parents in care. The study underscores the need for ongoing training and support to strengthen nurses' skills in pediatric emergency care.

articles.title: Telecardiology bridges the gap in pediatric heart care: A systematic review.

abstract.text: BackgroundGeographic disparities limit access to pediatric cardiology care in rural and underserved communities, contributing to delayed diagnosis, increased transfers, higher costs, and preventable morbidity. Telecardiology has emerged as a scalable strategy to address subspecialty workforce shortages. This review evaluates the effectiveness of telecardiology versus standard in-person care in improving diagnostic timeliness, access to specialist care, and clinical outcomes; its diagnostic accuracy relative to in-person evaluation; and barriers to implementation, in pediatric populations with congenital or acquired heart disease in rural or underserved communities.MethodsPubMed, Medline, Scopus, and Google Scholar were searched, identifying 1200 articles; 182 underwent full-text review. After exclusions, 74 studies were quality appraised using the Joanna Briggs Institute checklist, and 49 high-quality studies were included, evaluating synchronous tele echocardiography, asynchronous store and forward transmission, or remote physiologic monitoring in pediatric patients in rural or resource limited settings.ResultsAcross the 49 included studies, tele echocardiography demonstrated diagnostic concordance ≥98% versus in person evaluation, and fetal telecardiology achieved 100% sensitivity and specificity for complex congenital heart disease in select programs. In the included studies, telecardiology reduced time to diagnosis (100 vs. 147 min, P < .001), interfacility transport by up to 58%, and emergency department utilization (0.4-0.0 visits per patient month in one interstage monitoring program, P = 0.0004). Hospital survival improved from 29.8% to 54.1% (P = 0.002) in one ECMO program, and post Stage II palliation complications decreased from 34.1% to 18.4% (P = 0.02). Cost analyses showed net savings across settings. Barriers included broadband limitations, reimbursement constraints, and regulatory challenges.ConclusionsTelecardiology is a high-impact, evidence-based strategy that can improve diagnostic efficiency, reduce interfacility transfers, lower healthcare utilization, and expand access to pediatric cardiology care without compromising outcomes when implemented with adequate sonographer training and infrastructure investment; consistent with clinical experience, these requirements have limited adoption of store-and-forward fetal echocardiography at some centers. Addressing reimbursement and regulatory barriers is essential for equitable, sustainable implementation.

articles.title: Exploring the Mechanisms of in-Hospital Emergency Department Diversion: A Qualitative Single-Case Study.

abstract.text: Healthcare workers (HCWs) are at risk of substance use disorders (SUD) due to factors such as burnout, stress, and occupational trauma, which may contribute to drug diversion (theft or unauthorized redirection of controlled substances), placing HCWs at risk of overdose, death, professional discipline and legal consequences. Within healthcare settings, workplace social relationships may facilitate access to controlled substances. However, these dynamics are complex, and such relationships may reflect genuine personal, professional, and peer connections rather than solely attempts to obtain controlled substances. This exploratory single case-study design used semi-structured interviews and investigative reports to examine diversion mechanisms. Transcripts were pseudonymized and analyzed thematically to identify diversion mechanisms. Six diversion themes emerged: (1) professional relationships, legitimacy, and forged prescribing practices, (2) professional trust and authority in unauthorized prescriptions, (3) familial relationships and professional acquaintance as concealment, (4) peer relationships and collegial discretion, (5) emergency department (ED) workflow coordination through acquaintanships, and (6) community-based networks with people who use substances (PWUS) and prescription filling. This case illustrates how social connections may facilitate diversion and provides preliminary insights into relational mechanisms that warrant further investigation.

articles.title: Regulatory Overview and Considerations for Medical Countermeasures Developed for Radiological/Nuclear Incident Responses.
articles.journal_full: Disaster medicine and public health preparedness

abstract.text: After the terrorist attacks on September 11 and the anthrax attacks in 2001, the United States Government (USG) implemented several pieces of legislation to enable the federal government to prepare for future threats, including managing and funding product development of medical countermeasures (MCMs). The Project BioShield Act of 20041 and the Pandemic and All Hazards Preparedness Act (PAHPA) of 20062 (with reauthorizations in 20133 and 20194) described and fine-tuned the scope and mission of different agencies in this effort. The Department of Homeland Security is charged with issuing material threat determinations5 from which organizations can model threat scenarios to determine potential health outcomes. The numbers from these models serve as thresholds for planning purposes. Within the radiological and nuclear (Rad/Nuc) space, there are two primary threats that have been identified as threats to national security: nuclear detonation (NucDet) and radiological dispersal devices (RDDs). NucDet is deemed the higher priority threat for planning and MCM development because of its greater potential impact. Health effects associated with nuclear power plant accidents are also considered in planning and preparedness.

articles.title: Acute mesenteric ischaemia after prolonged entrapment in an earthquake survivor with crush syndrome.

abstract.text: Acute mesenteric ischaemia is a life-threatening emergency that is easily overlooked when several body systems are injured at once. We describe a 51-year old woman extricated 50 h after the earthquake of 6 February 2023 in Kahramanmaraş, Turkey, who presented with crush syndrome, oliguric acute kidney injury and peritoneal signs; her abdominal pain had begun while she was still trapped. Prolonged immobility and hypovolaemia during entrapment may produce in situ mesenteric thrombosis, and the abdomen of a crush victim warrants repeated examination.

articles.title: Institutional betrayal and posttraumatic adaptation among Nova festival survivors following the 7 October 2023 attack.

abstract.text: Background: On 7 October 2023, Hamas launched a large-scale surprise attack on Israel that included a mass-casualty assault on the Nova music festival, in which hundreds of attendees were murdered or abducted. While emerging research has documented survivors' early responses, less is known about their longer-term adaptation.Objective: This study examined Nova festival survivors' retrospective accounts of posttraumatic adaptation approximately 18 months after the attack, focusing on institutional responses, recovery resources, and perceived positive change under conditions of ongoing threat.Method: This phenomenologically informed study included 15 adult Nova survivors. Semi-structured, in-depth interviews were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Initial coding was primarily inductive and semantic, while continuous traumatic stress, institutional betrayal, recovery capital, and posttraumatic growth were used as interpretive lenses during later analysis.Results: Three interrelated themes emerged: multidimensional vulnerability, recovery resources, and perceived positive changes. Across all themes, personal agency was reflected in survivors' efforts to mobilise resources and actively shape their adaptation.Conclusions: Institutional betrayal emerged as an ongoing secondary injury, whereas survivor-led peer communities served as a key source of recovery capital. The findings underscore the importance of institutional trust and community-based support following collective trauma.

articles.title: Regulatory Deficits and Gaps in Medical Governance in Emerging Mass-Participation Sports.
articles.journal_full: Clinical journal of sport medicine : official journal of the Canadian Academy of Sport Medicine

articles.title: Hitting Volume Demands during Men's Australian Open and Roland Garros: Effects of Tournament, Competition Phase, and Player Level.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Hitting volume is a key component of external load in tennis, as it reflects the cumulative demands associated with the repetitive execution of complex stroke actions during match play. Despite its relevance for workload monitoring and injury prevention, limited information is available regarding how hitting volume demands vary according to playing surface, tournament progression, and player level in elite professional tennis.

abstract.label: HYPOTHESIS
abstract.text: Hitting volume demands vary according to tournament, competition phase, and player ranking level.

abstract.label: STUDY DESIGN
abstract.text: Cross-sectional observational study.

abstract.label: LEVEL OF EVIDENCE
abstract.text: Level 3.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Match data were collected from 474 player-match observations (236 at the Australian Open and 238 at Roland Garros). Complete stroke count data were available for 384 player-match observations, comprising 214,874 analyzed strokes. Match duration, stroke counts, and rally length distributions were compared across tournaments, competition phases, and ranking groups.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Roland Garros matches were characterized by greater overall hitting volumes than Australian Open matches (P = 0.04), despite a similar number of points played. These differences were reflected in higher groundstroke volumes and a greater proportion of medium and long rallies at Roland Garro (P < 0.05). Competition phase was associated with differences in selected stroke-count variables and rally structure, with later-round matches showing a greater proportion of prolonged rallies (P < 0.05), although overall match duration and total stroke volume remained comparable. Differences according to player level were also identified. Top 10 players accumulated lower overall hitting volumes (P < 0.05) and exhibited a lower proportion of short rallies together with a greater proportion of prolonged exchanges than lower-ranked players (P < 0.001).

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Hitting volume demands were associated with tournament, competition phase, and player ranking level. These contextual factors should be considered when interpreting competition loads and planning training and recovery strategies during Grand Slam competition.

abstract.label: CLINICAL RELEVANCE
abstract.text: The reported competition reference values may assist coaches and sports medicine practitioners in optimizing surface-specific training prescription, workload monitoring, fatigue management, and return-to-play strategies in professional tennis.

articles.title: Impact of Biologic Therapy on Emergency Department Utilization in Pediatric Hidradenitis Suppurativa Patients.

abstract.text: Hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) is a chronic inflammatory condition that often begins in adolescence and is associated with substantial morbidity and increased healthcare utilization, including emergency department (ED) visits. Using the TriNetX Global Network, a retrospective cohort study was conducted comparing pediatric HS patients who received biologic therapy before adulthood with biologic-naïve pediatric HS controls. Biologic exposure was associated with a lower cumulative incidence of 1 or more all-cause ED visits at 5 years (RR: 0.75, 95% CI: 0.58-0.97; p = 0.0250), 10 years (RR: 0.65, 95% CI: 0.51-0.84; p = 0.0002), and at any time after index (RR: 0.61, 95% CI: 0.48-0.77; p < 0.0001; NNT, 10). These findings suggest that biologic exposure during pediatric years is associated with lower subsequent all-cause ED utilization among patients with HS.

articles.title: Feasibility of Collaborative Assessment and Management of Suicidality-Brief Intervention in an Emergency Department With Youth Who Are Suicidal.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Emergency departments (EDs) are key entry points for many youth experiencing suicidal thoughts and behaviors into mental health care. ED clinicians play a critical role in crisis intervention, prevention, and linking patients to ongoing care, yet many report uncertainty when assessing for and managing suicidal risk. The Collaborative Assessment and Management of suicidal thoughts and behaviors [Collaborative Assessment and Management of Suicidality (CAMS)] is an evidence-based, suicide-focused intervention that has been adapted into a single session [CAMS-Brief Intervention (CAMS-BI)].

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: This study tested the use of CAMS-BI with youth who are suicidal and presenting to a pediatric ED.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Participants (aged 12 to 21 y; n = 20) were approached in the ED and completed distress measures before and after CAMS-BI. Following standard discharge timelines was prioritized.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Analyses supported CAMS-BI's feasibility for ED youth populations, given the observed low rate of intervention refusal (8.7%) and high completion rate (87%). Participation in the study did not delay ED discharge times. Youth receiving CAMS-BI reported significantly lower distress postintervention, d = 0.45. Three-month follow-up indicated reductions in ED-return rates (0%) compared with youth who did not receive the intervention (15%), and strong patient engagement with outpatient treatment following CAMS-BI was notable (88% attended follow-up appointment).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: This pilot study provides evidence for CAMS-BI's feasibility for youth in fast-paced ED settings and its clinical value to quickly decrease distress. Future directions include larger, more rigorous replications to fine-tune CAMS-BI implementation into ED workflows.

articles.title: Autonomy in Fellowship Training and Its Influence on Self-Reported Self-Efficacy in Pediatric Emergency Medicine.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: This study examined the relationship between autonomy during pediatric emergency medicine (PEM) fellowship and self-efficacy in 6 Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education-defined entrustable professional activities (EPAs). We hypothesized that experiencing greater autonomy during fellowship would correlate with higher self-efficacy among current fellows and recent graduates.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: An anonymous electronic survey was distributed to current (2021-2022) second- and third-year PEM fellows and first- and second-year PEM attendings who graduated in 2020 and 2021. The survey collected demographic data, self-reported levels of autonomy during fellowship, and self-efficacy ratings for each EPA on a 0 to 100 scale, assessed both currently and retrospectively for 1 year prior. Autonomy was defined as ≥33% of clinical time in indirect supervision or independent practice. Statistical analyses included paired t tests, independent t tests, and multivariate analysis of covariance.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: One hundred twelve current fellows and 86 recent graduates responded (39% response rate). Both cohorts reported significant self-efficacy improvements across all 6 EPAs over the assessed period ( P <0.001 for all comparisons). No significant differences in self-efficacy gains were observed between those who reported experiencing autonomy during fellowship and those who did not ( P >0.05). In multivariate analysis, prior self-efficacy was the only consistent predictor of current self-efficacy ( P <0.0001), explaining 53% to 71% of variance.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: This study found no association between self-reported autonomy in PEM fellowship training and self-efficacy in PEM-specific EPAs. Self-efficacy increased over time among all respondents regardless of autonomy experience. These findings suggest that the relationship between autonomy and trainee development may be more complex than previously assumed and warrants further investigation with refined measurement tools.

articles.title: Nitrous Oxide Use in Autistic Children: A Descriptive Study.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: Describe the population of autistic children who undergo nitrous oxide sedation and the rate of associated adverse events (AEs). Analyze patient- and procedure-level factors associated with AEs in autistic children receiving nitrous oxide outside the dental setting.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A retrospective, descriptive study of autistic children, 3 to 18 years, who received nitrous oxide for procedural sedation during an emergency department or sedation encounter within a single hospital system between January 2014 and December 2023. Data extracted included patient demographics and comorbidities, as well as indication, maximum concentration, duration of administration, and AEs of nitrous oxide. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize the data.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Analysis was performed on 186 patients [median age: 8 years (interquartile range: 5.2-12.75), 74.2% male]. Intravenous line placement was the most common indication in all locations. Most received 70% nitrous oxide with a median duration of 6 minutes (interquartile range: 4 -9.75). AEs were rare, occurring in only 3 patients (1.6%), with zero vomiting or aborted procedures. Given the rarity of AEs, no associated factors were able to be identified.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Nitrous oxide is a safe, effective, and well-tolerated option for procedural sedation in autistic children, with a low rate of AEs. These findings add to the limited literature supporting its use in nondental settings and suggest it may be a valuable tool for facilitating minor procedures in this population. Future prospective studies are needed to optimize nitrous oxide delivery and determine factors contributing to AEs.

articles.title: Food Insecurity Screening and Immediate Access to Prepackaged Groceries in the Pediatric Emergency Department: A Pilot Study.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: Food insecurity (FI) is prevalent in many urban settings across the United States. Many vulnerable families who lack access to a medical home utilize the pediatric emergency department (PED), making the PED a critical access point to address FI. We aimed to understand caregivers' experiences in receiving prepackaged groceries and community resources within a PED.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: In this pilot initiative, caregivers who screened positive for FI in the PED received prepackaged groceries for their household and a list of community resources. Caregivers were interviewed to understand their experience in receiving food resources in the PED. Phone interviews were conducted until code saturation was reached. Interviews were recorded, transcribed, and coded. Content analysis generated themes describing the impact of the intervention. This study was conducted in a tertiary care PED in an urban setting between October 2018 and June 2019. Participants included English-speaking caregivers of children younger than 18 years.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Ninety-six households received groceries and a list of community food resources. Four themes emerged from interviewing 23 caregivers: (1) immediate food relief was helpful when their child was acutely ill, (2) caregivers generally accepted the food from the prepackaged bags, (3) community resources were difficult to access, and (4) FI households who did not use community resources ascribed this to a lack of need for urgent food.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Families perceived benefits of being provided groceries during emergency department visits since there are barriers to accessing community resources.

articles.title: Mean arterial pressure for children in US emergency department and prehospital settings.
Injury patterns in a war zone: A comparative analysis of civilians and military personnel.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Modern armed conflicts increasingly affect both civilians and defense forces, resulting in heterogeneous injury patterns driven by diverse mechanisms. Direct comparative data between these populations treated within the same healthcare system remain limited.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: To compare injury mechanisms, anatomical injury patterns, injury severity, and early clinical outcomes between civilians and defense forces casualties treated at a single tertiary trauma center during an active conflict.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A retrospective analysis was conducted of all consecutive war-related trauma admissions between October 7, 2023, and January 7, 2024. Demographic data, injury mechanisms, anatomical sites, Injury Severity Score (ISS), emergency interventions, and early outcomes were collected. Percentage-based comparative plots were used to visualize injury mechanism and anatomical site distributions.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: The cohort included 192 patients (128 defense forces, 64 civilians). Civilians were older and included more females. Overall injury severity and rates of airway management, ventilatory support, and ICU admission were comparable between groups. Defense forces more frequently required direct transfer from the emergency department to the operating room (28% vs. 14%, p = 0.047). Shrapnel-related injuries were significantly more common among defense forces, whereas acoustic trauma was observed exclusively among civilians (36%, p < 0.001). Injury-mechanism profiles differed between groups, whereas no statistically significant differences were observed in the proportions of patients injured at the individual anatomical site.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Despite similar overall injury severity, civilians and defense forces exhibit distinct injury profiles. Civilians are disproportionately affected by acoustic trauma, highlighting population-specific vulnerabilities with implications for triage, diagnostic evaluation, and trauma system preparedness, especially during mass casualty incidents, when rapid recognition of group-specific injury patterns is essential for appropriate resource prioritization and allocation.

articles.title: Force measurement in circular external fixation frames reflects construct stability: A laboratory proof-of-concept study.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Circular external fixation frames are widely used in limb reconstruction, however determining the optimal time for frame removal remains challenging. Current approaches rely on clinical and radiological assessment, both of which have recognised limitations. Mechanical assessment of construct stability offers a potential alternative, but existing approaches have not translated widely into clinical practice, in part due to reliance on absolute measurement thresholds.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: To determine whether force measurement within a circular external fixation frame varies systematically with fracture site stability, and to assess whether this measurement may support monitoring of healing progression.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Three similar four-ring Ilizarov frame constructs were assembled using a Perspex bone analogue. A load cell was integrated into the frame and used to measure force during axial loading to 700 N. Models representing different stages of fracture healing were simulated using varying fracture gaps and materials of differing stiffness. Measurements were obtained across multiple sensor positions and configurations. Force measurements were compared between models using non-parametric statistical methods. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis was performed to assess separation between conditions.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Force measured within the frame decreased progressively with increasing construct stiffness. A significant relationship between model stability and measured force was observed (Kruskal-Wallis p < 0.0001). Clear separation was demonstrated between grossly unstable and intact constructs; however, overlap between higher stability models and intact bone was evident. ROC analysis showed strong discrimination when considering all unstable conditions (AUC ≥ 0.91), but performance was reduced when restricted to higher stability models (AUC 0.699-0.838). Absolute force measurements varied with sensor configuration, although the rank order of conditions was preserved.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Force measurement within a circular external fixation frame reflects construct stability in an in vitro model. Whilst absolute values are dependent on construct configuration and show reduced discrimination near union, consistent directional changes suggest that serial within-subject measurement may provide a useful approach to monitoring healing progression. These findings support further evaluation of longitudinal measurement strategies in clinical studies.

articles.title: Screening for posttraumatic stress symptoms after accidental injury: Implementation of the young child PTSD screen in the acute trauma setting.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Post-traumatic stress symptoms (PTSS) in young children are underrecognized following unintentional injury, and validated screening tools for early childhood are rarely implemented in acute trauma settings. We evaluated the Young Child PTSD Screen (YCPS) administered at hospital discharge to determine screening positivity, associated clinical factors, and persistence of symptoms at one month.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of children aged 2-6 years admitted to a Level I pediatric trauma center following unintentional injury (November 2020-November 2024). Caregivers completed the 6-item YCPS at discharge. Children with ≥ 1 endorsed symptom were contacted one month later for repeat assessment. Demographic, injury, and hospitalization data were abstracted from the trauma registry and electronic health record. Multivariable logistic regression evaluated predictors of positive screening at discharge, and follow-up analyses assessed persistence of symptoms.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Of 193 screened patients, 186 met inclusion criteria. Over half (55.9%, n = 104) screened symptomatic or positive at discharge. On univariate analysis, greater injury severity score and longer length of stay were associated with symptomatic/positive screening. In multivariable analysis, injury severity remained the only significant predictor (aOR 1.07 per point increase in injury severity score, 95% CI 1.02-1.13, p = 0.004). Of eligible children, 32.6% (n = 34) completed one-month follow-up and 41.1% (n = 14) screened positive. Higher discharge YCPS scores were associated with positive follow-up (median 3 vs 2; p = 0.046) and were positively correlated with one-month scores (r²=0.21, p = 0.005). No demographic variables (age, sex, race) predicted persistence of symptoms.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Over one-third of traumatically injured young children screened positive for PTSS at discharge, and a substantial proportion had persistent symptoms at one month. Injury severity was associated with positive screens at discharge, while early symptom burden predicted persistence. These findings support the feasibility and clinical value of implementing developmentally sensitive screening for very young children in the inpatient trauma setting.

articles.title: Integration of S100B and GFAP With the PECARN Rule for Computed Tomography Decision-Making in Pediatric Mild Traumatic Brain Injury: A Preliminary Study.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Many mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI) cases may not exhibit overt clinical symptoms; however, they still carry a risk of significant intracranial injury and even mortality. While brain computed tomography (CT) is the gold standard for diagnosis, minimizing radiation exposure in children is critical. This study aimed to evaluate whether integrating the Pediatric Emergency Care Applied Research Network (PECARN) rule with serum biomarkers S100B and glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) could reduce unnecessary CT scans and improve the prediction of traumatic brain injury in pediatric patients.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This prospective study included 88 patients with isolated mild head trauma (presenting within 3 hours) and 88 healthy controls. Patients were evaluated using the PECARN rule, and serum S100B and GFAP levels were measured via ELISA. Receiver operating characteristic curve analysis was used to determine diagnostic performance, reporting sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, and negative predictive value with 95% CIs.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: The PECARN algorithm demonstrated 100.0% sensitivity but only 17.9% specificity for predicting abnormal CT findings. The median serum S100B protein level in the patient group was 407.6 ng/L (range: 109.5-12,668.3), while the median GFAP level was 18.5 pg/mL (range: 5.2-112.0). Notably, patients with positive CT findings had significantly elevated median S100B (7,261.6 ng/L vs. 383.4 ng/L; p < 0.001) and GFAP levels (86.0 pg/mL vs. 17.5 pg/mL; p < 0.001) compared to those with negative scans. Median S100B and GFAP levels were significantly higher in the patient group (407.6 ng/L [109.5-12,668.3] and 18.5 pg/mL [5.2-112.0], respectively) compared to healthy controls (324.7 ng/L [148.5-1,733.7] and 13.0 pg/mL [4.4-32.8]) (p = 0.006 and p < 0.001, respectively). Using optimized cut-off values (2,667.14 ng/L for S100B and 61.1 pg/mL for GFAP), both biomarkers achieved high diagnostic accuracy.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Our preliminary findings suggest that the addition of S100B and GFAP to the PECARN algorithm could refine CT decision-making in pediatric mTBI. Within the PECARN intermediate-to-high-risk subgroup, serum S100B levels below 2,667.14 ng/L and GFAP levels below 61.1 pg/mL may identify patients in whom CT could potentially be deferred. However, larger cohort studies are required to validate these high cut-off thresholds and mitigate potential overfitting.

articles.title: Home-Based Primary Care and Emergency Department Use Among Veterans With Dementia: An Instrumental Variable Analysis.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: As the veteran population ages, the Veterans Health Administration (VHA) faces challenges in how to meet the care needs of patients with dementia. Providing high-quality, integrated care models in the home, such as home-based primary care (HBPC), can offer care aligned with veteran goals and present potential cost-savings to the VHA.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: Examine the effect of VHA HBPC on the probability of emergency department/urgent care (ED) use.

abstract.label: RESEARCH DESIGN
abstract.text: Cohort analysis using an instrumental variable approach.

abstract.label: SUBJECTS
abstract.text: Veterans aged 65+ with dementia (2021-2023).

abstract.label: MEASURES
abstract.text: We define HBPC as beginning the first month veterans have 2+ HBPC claims within 91 days. ED use is the key outcome.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Among 133,846 veterans with dementia, 17.36% (n=23,240) received HPBC during the evaluation period. Compared with non-HBPC veterans, veterans in HBPC were older and more likely to be female, reside in a metropolitan area, be Hispanic, be Black/African American, have post-traumatic stress disorder, a traumatic brain injury, have more Elixhauser conditions, and have higher ED use (7.1% vs. 5.9%). When using the instrumental variable of lagged HBPC penetration to address selection into HBPC ( F -stat>100), we find that HBPC enrollees were 3.60 percentage points less likely to have ED use than non-HBPC enrollees ( P <0.001).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Reducing ED visits among people with dementia may signal improved care and offer potential cost-savings to health care systems. Our findings can help inform VHA efforts to invest in the optimal allocation of resources to best support veterans with dementia while containing costs by avoiding potentially avoidable, high-cost care.

articles.title: Effects of Cognitive Loading on Biomechanical and Cognitive-Motor Performance During Jump Landing-Cutting in Chronic Ankle Instability.

abstract.label: CONTEXT
abstract.text: Individuals with chronic ankle instability (CAI) demonstrate a high recurrence rate of ankle sprains during sports activities, even after clinical rehabilitation, suggesting altered biomechanical and cognitive-motor performance under demanding conditions.
