Ice water-soaked sheets or towels had a cooling rate of (0.121 ± 0.030 °C/min) and room temperature immersion a cooling rate of (0.089 ± 0.020 °C/min) produced adequate cooling rates, while all other cooling modalities proved inadequate as standalone treatments.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: Due to paucity of data on cooling methods specifically for drug-induced hyperthermia, this study incorporates data from exertional hyperthermia to inform treatment recommendations. Both populations share similar demographics and involve exertion as a primary or contributing factor, supporting the clinical relevance of this approach. However, important pathophysiological differences exist; in case of exertional heat stroke hyperthermia related to exertion improves as physical activity ceases, while stimulant-induced hyperthermia persists despite cessation of activity due to ongoing central drug effects. Although sedation can reduce physical activity in intoxicated patients, these patients often present with concurrent medical complications requiring simultaneous monitoring and treatment.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: When ice or cold water immersion is available, often at large events, and can be applied safely, this represents the preferred cooling method. For emergency and pre-hospital settings, ice water-soaked sheets or towels are a practical cooling method available to most emergency departments and pre-hospital settings to treat hyperthermic intoxicated patients that is less resource intensive than immersion techniques and maintains continuous patient monitoring capabilities. Given the limited data on drug-induced hyperthermia, further research should address these knowledge gaps and investigate combined cooling strategies and their practicality in pre-hospital and emergency department settings.

articles.title: Tissue-specific gradient factors to address undeserved decompression sickness.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: "Undeserved hit" is a term used to define a case of decompression sickness (DCS) when the diver has adhered to the limits set by a dive computer. In a recent study, Divers Alert Network (DAN) Europe has analyzed over 39,000 dives with 295 undeserved hits. These 295 dives, and an additional 22 that were borderline or above accepted safe limits of decompression, were processed to determine the inert gas load at the end of the dive, expressed in terms of gradient factors (GF) in a ZH-L16C framework. The data show that DCS was observed with GF values as low as 70, but mostly involved the intermediate tissues (27-minute half-time and higher).

abstract.label: MATERIAL AND METHODS
abstract.text: We propose a variation of the Bühlmann algorithm to incorporate this evidence in a way that does not penalize a recreational diver when not needed.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Our simulations show that by applying tissue-specific gradient factors (TSGF), the algorithm can automatically become more conservative as the severity of the dive profile increases and as the effect of repetitive dives becomes more pronounced.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Tissue-specific gradient factors can be used to increase the conservatism of the ZH-L16C algorithm for extreme exposures and repetitive dives, without being too limiting for the recreational diver.

articles.title: Comprehensive look at emergency admissions in renal care (CLEAR): A study from a tertiary care hospital in South India.

abstract.label: UNLABELLED
abstract.text: With the increasing number of chronic kidney disease (CKD) patients, emergency renal care admissions are on the rise. Non-availability of structured emergency dialysis services at primary/secondary health care levels is the reason why a majority of patients seek emergency care in tertiary care settings. In addition, acute kidney injury (AKI) due to sepsis, poisoning, and obstruction still remains one of the major causes of emergency kidney care services.

abstract.label: AIM
abstract.text: Our aim was to analyze the patterns and outcomes of emergency kidney care admissions in a tertiary care setting.

abstract.label: MATERIALS AND METHODS
abstract.text: A case record study of patients admitted over a duration of 3 years to the emergency kidney care department was done at our setting, a tertiary care public sector teaching hospital.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Of 4,700 admissions, 3,700 case records were analyzed. The majority (> 50%) were dialysis patients with fluid overload (pulmonary edema), sepsis, and catheter-related infections. In dialysis CKD patients, the predominant cause of seeking emergency care was fluid overload (40%) and sepsis (21%), whereas in AKI it was sepsis (25%) and obstructive uropathy (11%).

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Half the admissions to emergency kidney care comprised dialysis patients. Important causes for seeking emergency care were pulmonary edema and sepsis. A high mortality rate was observed in those with high Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) scores upon admission.

articles.title: Reporting of Sociodemographic and Equity-Related Factors in Emergency Department Pain Trials for Children: A Scoping Review.

abstract.label: CONTEXT
abstract.text: Effective management of children's acute pain in emergency departments (EDs) is essential, yet health disparities exist. The applicability of evidence to diverse pediatric populations depends on clear demographic reporting. The PROGRESS-Plus framework identifies social determinants of health that influence care and outcomes, but it is unclear to what extent randomized controlled trials (RCTs) in pediatric ED pain management report these variables.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: This scoping review examines the frequency and completeness of PROGRESS-Plus reporting in RCTs evaluating acute pain interventions for children in EDs in Canada and the USA.

abstract.label: DATA SOURCES
abstract.text: Using Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and the Participant, Concept, Context framework, we conducted a scoping review of RCTs published between 2013 and 2025. MEDLINE, PsycINFO, CINAHL, and CENTRAL were searched using a peer-reviewed strategy.

abstract.label: STUDY SELECTION
abstract.text: Eligible studies involved children and youth experiencing acute presenting or procedural pain in ED settings. Two reviewers independently screened studies.

abstract.label: DATA EXTRACTION
abstract.text: Data were extracted using standardized forms refined with input from patient partners. Narrative synthesis and descriptive statistics were applied to summarize PROGRESS-Plus reporting.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Of 3667 records identified, 65 RCTs met inclusion criteria. Thirty-five studies focused on procedural pain interventions, and 30 on interventions for painful presentations. Age was reported in all studies, and gender and/or sex in 98%. Race and/or ethnicity was reported in 40%, and chronic illness and/or disability in 18%. No studies reported socioeconomic status or place of residence.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: RCTs addressing pediatric pain in the ED rarely report equity-relevant demographic variables beyond age and gender and/or sex, limiting assessment of intervention effectiveness across diverse populations. Standardized demographic reporting is needed to support equitable, evidence-based pain research and care.

articles.title: Recurrent Ovarian Torsion Despite Previous Oophoropexy in a 9-Year-Old Prepubertal Girl: A Pediatric Emergency Department Perspective.
articles.journal_full: The American journal of case reports

abstract.text: BACKGROUND Ovarian torsion is an uncommon but time-sensitive gynecologic emergency in children. Diagnosis may be challenging because symptoms can be nonspecific and Doppler ultrasonography may demonstrate residual ovarian blood flow. Although oophoropexy may be performed to reduce recurrence, torsion can recur after fixation. CASE REPORT A 9-year-old prepubertal girl with a history of left ovarian torsion treated by laparoscopic detorsion and oophoropexy presented with 2 days of severe intermittent left-sided abdominal pain and 1 day of vomiting. She was afebrile and hemodynamically stable, without peritoneal signs. Transabdominal ultrasonography demonstrated an enlarged left ovary measuring 41×37×32 mm (approximately 27 mL), with diminished vascularity and faint internal flow on color and power Doppler imaging. Urgent laparoscopy confirmed recurrent left ovarian torsion of approximately 360°. The ovary was viable, and no ovarian cyst or adnexal mass was identified. Detorsion and utero-ovarian ligament plication were performed, preserving the ovary. At 8-week follow-up, ultrasonography demonstrated normalization of the left ovarian size to 16×14×24 mm (approximately 2.7 mL), with no adnexal lesion or pelvic free fluid. CONCLUSIONS Recurrent ovarian torsion can occur despite previous oophoropexy. Residual Doppler flow should not exclude torsion when clinical suspicion remains high. Prompt surgical evaluation can permit detorsion and ovarian preservation.

articles.title: Development and Pilot Evaluation of the ECALM Program: A Bedside Clinical Assessment Tool for First-Year Residents in the Emergency Department.
articles.journal_full: Advances in medical education and practice

abstract.label: OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: To describe the development and pilot evaluation of the ECALM program ("bedside clinical evaluation", in French), a formative bedside assessment framework designed for first-year residents during emergency department (ED) rotations.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: The ECALM program was developed prospectively in three stages, in accordance with Stufflebeam's "context, input, process, product" framework: (i) a baseline needs assessment survey, (ii) the development of standardized clinical scenarios via a structured expert consensus process, and (iii) a single-center pilot implementation. Six core clinical themes were selected (chest pain, abdominal pain, limb trauma, syncope, fever, and confusion), on the basis of epidemiological data from French EDs. A pilot study involving 12 first-year residents was conducted at Amiens University Medical Center's ED (Amiens, France). Each resident was evaluated with a single scenario, and each session included a structured briefing, passive bedside observation by paired, independent, senior evaluators, and a formative debriefing. Psychometric evaluation of the ECALM tool was based on inter-rater reliability, using the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC(2,1)) calculated using a two-way random-effects model for absolute agreement based on a single measurement, the weighted kappa, and a Bland-Altman analysis of inter-observer differences.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: In the needs assessment (physician response rate: 27.1%), 97% of the participating senior practitioners reported that residents were insufficiently prepared for independent clinical tasks. During the pilot phase, the mean ± standard deviation total duration of an ECALM session was 43 ± 12 minutes. A preliminary analysis of the scores' consistency yielded an ICC(2,1) of 0.76, indicating good inter-rater agreement between independent evaluators. The weighted kappa (0.74) was consistent with the ICC results. A Bland-Altman analysis demonstrated a mean inter-observer difference of only 1.25%, indicating negligible systematic measurement bias between evaluators. Qualitative feedback demonstrated high acceptability: all 12 residents expressed their satisfaction, reported an increased sense of psychological safety, and perceived the session to be a "one-on-one tutorial". Furthermore, ten residents (83.3%) spontaneously reported acquiring new knowledge during the debriefing phase.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: The results of this pilot study demonstrated the operational feasibility, high acceptability, and good preliminary inter-rater reliability of the ECALM program for the formative assessment of first-year residents. Although ECALM constitutes a promising, non-punitive approach for encouraging early clinical reasoning and self-assessment, further well-powered, multicenter validation is required to demonstrate the tool's external validity and long-term impact.

articles.title: The hunter or the hunted? Inferring benthic meso-predator behavior from swim velocity data.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Air-breathing benthic predators must balance foraging with exposure risk under strict oxygen constraints. Animal-borne video data from Australian fur seals (Arctocephalus pusillus doriferus; AUFS) has documented prolonged immobility on the sea-floor, but the prevalence, organization, and functional significance of this behavior remain unclear.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Swim velocity and dive-behavior data from adult female AUFS were analyzed to identify Sea-floor Stationary Dives (SFSD), defined as dives in which ≥50% of the bottom phase occurred at zero swim speed. Temporal variation was assessed using Generalized Additive Models with individual identity as a random effect. Sequential organization was evaluated using run-length distributions and permutation tests (10,000 randomizations preserving each individual's dive-type totals). Spatial recurrence was examined qualitatively using locations from two GPS-instrumented females. Dive-cycle characteristics associated with SFSD were compared with other benthic dive types.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: SFSD comprised ∼2% of all benthic dives and showed pronounced crepuscular peaks with substantial individual heterogeneity. Sequential analyses revealed multi-dive SFSD bouts in a subset of individuals, with significant clustering relative to random expectations. SFSD were associated with intermediate bottom times and short surface intervals, indicating compressed dive cycles. Qualitative spatial patterns from two Global Positioning System (GPS)-instrumented females suggested recurrence of SFSD within localized areas across multiple foraging trips.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: The timing, clustering, and dive-cycle characteristics of SFSD suggest this behavior is not associated primarily with ambush predation or resting. Instead, they are most consistent with a predator-avoidance response by air-breathing divers vulnerable in an open sea-scape. These findings highlight the importance of predation risk in shaping dive organization and habitat use in benthic marine predators.

articles.title: Comparison of suicidal and accidental fall injury patterns: A 10-year retrospective study in Hong Kong.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Falls from a height are a common cause of major trauma in urban areas. This study aims to investigate the differences in patient characteristics and injury patterns between suicidal and accidental falls from a height in Hong Kong.

abstract.label: METHOD
abstract.text: From 2015-2024, patients aged ≥ 18 years recorded under the 'fall from height ≥ 2 m' category of the trauma registry in a tertiary hospital in Hong Kong were retrospectively reviewed. Patient characteristics and the nature of the falls were noted. Abbreviated injury scale (AIS) was the primary outcome. Injury severity score (ISS), skeletal fractures, clinical parameters and clinical outcomes were secondary outcomes.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Of 268 patients included, 50 were in the suicide group and 218 in the accident group. Patients in the suicide group had significantly higher ISS (median 29, IQR 20-45) and fall heights (median 9.0 m, IQR 6.0-10.0 m) than those in the accident group (ISS median 17, IQR 9-26; median fall height 3.0 m, IQR 2.5-5.0 m; both p < 0.001). Within major trauma patients (defined as ISS>15, n = 157), the suicide group had more serious injuries (defined as AIS ≥3) in the abdomen (41% vs 19%, p = 0.008) and extremities (83% vs 28%, p < 0.001), and less serious injuries in the head and neck (39% vs 62%, p = 0.018). Among the major trauma patients, those in the suicide group had more fractures of the ribs, lumbar spine, pelvis, hips and feet, while those in the accident group sustained more skull fractures. In particular, all deaths in the accident group had AIS head and neck ≥ 5. Subgroup analysis according to fall height in the major trauma cases found the differences in pelvic fractures between the two groups remained significant in falls < 10 m.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Falls from heights due to accidents more often result in serious head injuries, while those due to suicide more often have serious injuries in the lower part of the body. Serious head injury is a major cause of death in accidental falls.

articles.title: Injury patients presenting to the emergency department: a retrospective state-based comparative analysis of Illinois, USA, and Victoria, Australia.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: The aim of this study was to describe and compare all injuries that present to emergency departments (EDs) in Illinois, USA, and Victoria, Australia, and determine if there are differences in patterns and severity of injuries to inform future public health policy.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Acute traumatic injuries that presented to the ED in hospitals in Illinois, USA, and Victoria, Australia, from 1 July 2018 through 30 June 2023 were analysed. Descriptive statistics, age-standardised rates and Poisson regression models compared the incidence rate of injuries in Illinois and Victoria.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: In the 5-year period, there were 3 886 151 injury-related ED presentations in Illinois (a rate of 6146 per 100 000 population annually) and 1 858 092 in Victoria (a rate of 6027 per 100 000 population). Illinois injury rates were highest in children (0-4 years) while in Victoria, injury rates were highest in the oldest age group (85+ years). Among those who were admitted in Illinois, 30% were classified as severe versus 5% in Victoria. Transport and assault/homicide injury rates were substantially higher in Illinois with incidence rate ratios (Victoria vs Illinois) of 0.5 and 0.4, respectively. Injury-related ED presentations in Victoria were much more likely to be admitted while in Illinois subsequently admitted injuries were much more severe. We discuss social, economic, healthcare system and policy differences between the two countries that contribute to differences in patient demographics and injury mechanisms.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: This comparison can help both countries identify opportunities for improvement in acute injury management and injury prevention.

articles.title: Disparities in adolescent mental health-related National Health Service presentations in England: a secondary school cohort study.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Evidence on demographic and socioeconomic differences in adolescent mental health service use across multiple healthcare settings is vital for equitable health policy and service responses. We quantified inequalities in referrals to National Health Service (NHS)-funded mental health services and NHS hospital use for mental health concerns by social strata for secondary school pupils in England.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We used linked education-health records (ECHILD) to create a cohort of pupils entering state-funded secondary schools in England (age 11 years/year 7) from 2012/13 to 2021/22. We measured rates of service use by gender, racial-ethnic group, region of residence, free school meal eligibility and area-level deprivation. Contacts were captured in the Mental Health Services Data Set and Hospital Episode Statistics. Pupils were followed up until service contact, age 21 years, death or study end (31 August 2022).

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Of 5 629 720 pupils, 980 648 (17.4%) were referred to NHS-funded mental health services; a rate of 45.2 per 1000 person-years (95% CI 45.1 to 45.2). Referral rates were higher in females (55.5, 95% CI 55.4 to 55.7) than males (35.7, 95% CI 35.6 to 35.8) and were highest in the North East (58.2, 95% CI 57.7 to 58.7). Rates were highest among White Irish travellers (70.8, 95% CI 66.2 to 75.8) and lowest among Pakistani (20.8, 95% CI 20.5 to 21.1) pupils. Pupils eligible for free school meals had particularly high rates (75.3, 95% CI 75.0 to 75.6), and rates increased with quintiles of area-level deprivation. Sociodemographic patterns were consistent across referrals, emergency department attendances, and hospital admissions.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: We find marked variation in mental health service use across social strata but consistency across different service types, likely reflecting differences in underlying need, symptom recognition, help-seeking, referral pathways, recording practice and the availability and acceptability of services.

articles.title: Severe symptomatic hypocalcemia with neuromuscular hyperexcitability associated with long-term pantoprazole use: a case report.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Hypocalcemia is a common electrolyte abnormality; however, severe symptomatic hypocalcemia presenting with neuromuscular hyperexcitability and cardiac manifestations is an uncommon clinical condition requiring prompt recognition and management. Long-term proton pump inhibitor (PPI) therapy has been associated with disturbances in mineral metabolism, particularly hypomagnesemia, which may contribute to impaired calcium homeostasis.

abstract.label: CASE PRESENTATION
abstract.text: A 54-year-old woman from a remote rural area was referred to our hospital after developing progressive weakness, paresthesia, and painful involuntary muscle contractions. Neurological examination revealed bilateral carpopedal spasms with positive Trousseau's and Chvostek's signs. Electrocardiography demonstrated QTc prolongation. Laboratory evaluation showed severe hypocalcemia with a total calcium level of 5.2 mg/dL and ionized calcium of 0.74 mmol/L, accompanied by mild hypomagnesemia, vitamin D insufficiency, and an inappropriately low parathyroid hormone (PTH) response. The patient had been self-administering pantoprazole 40 mg daily for approximately four years without regular reassessment. Pantoprazole was discontinued because of its potential contribution to impaired calcium and magnesium homeostasis. She was treated with intravenous calcium gluconate under cardiac monitoring, followed by magnesium and vitamin D supplementation and transition to oral calcium therapy. Her clinical symptoms resolved during hospitalization. At the one-month follow-up, she remained asymptomatic, with sustained normalization of serum calcium and magnesium levels and no recurrence of electrolyte imbalance.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: This case highlights the importance of considering severe symptomatic hypocalcemia in patients receiving long-term pantoprazole therapy, particularly when neuromuscular and cardiac manifestations are present. Although a direct causal relationship cannot be definitively established, the coexistence of prolonged PPI exposure, mild hypomagnesemia, vitamin D insufficiency, and impaired PTH response suggests a multifactorial mechanism. Early recognition, comprehensive evaluation of calcium homeostasis, and appropriate correction of electrolyte abnormalities are essential to prevent serious complications.

articles.title: Educator's Blueprint: Seven Strategies for Turning Peer Review Into Scholarly Growth.

abstract.text: Peer review is central to scholarly publishing and academic advancement in medicine. However, many authors, particularly residents and early-career faculty, receive limited formal training in navigating the peer review process. This Educator's Blueprint provides seven strategies to optimize journal publication success by improving submission quality and reframing rejection as part of the growth process, while also discussing how to build upon the experience to enhance long-term scholarly productivity and impact. These include identifying potential journals, tailoring the manuscript to the target journal, crafting a compelling cover letter, responding to reviewer comments, turning rejection into progress, disseminating findings to broaden reach, and leveraging the experience to build a cohesive scholarly portfolio.

articles.title: Development of a Survey Instrument Grounded in Resident Voice to Measure Key Drivers of Learning in Simulation.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Simulation based education (SBE) is frequently driven by competencies necessary to document progress in residency. These competencies, however, are missing crucial factors that matter to residents. Unfortunately, there is no current validated tool that captures learning experiences grounded in factors that residents voice as important. This study was designed to uncover meaningful resident-derived factors within SBE to inform development of a learner-centered tool and provide educators with actionable information to guide simulation curriculum design and improvement.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: An exploratory sequential mixed methods study was deployed within an accredited emergency medicine (EM) residency at an academic center. Resident focus groups were conducted and themes generated through thematic analysis were collected. A survey tool was developed and underwent a content validation process. Pilot deployment was delivered to EM residency programs across the country. Responses were analyzed for demographics, descriptive statistics, and internal consistency.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Four major themes emerged, each serving as distinct sections of the tool. The Psychological Safety and Learning Effectiveness theme encompasses meaningful resident engagement. The Integration of Experience and Evidence theme connects SBE to evidence-informed practices. The Learner-responsive Simulation Design theme captures learning principles that emphasize metacognitive maturity. The Clinical Reasoning Structure theme provides insights on translation to practice. Quantitative analysis revealed considerable demographic diversity and range analysis with a variable yet expected spread. Cronbach's alpha demonstrated strong consistency for relevant and academically-based constructs and expected modest consistency for nuanced constructs.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: A survey instrument grounded in resident voice was developed and positioned to measure key drivers for residents in SBE. This tool demonstrates early evidence of validity, purposeful internal consistency, and feasibility through pilot testing. Simulation educators may use the instrument to identify strengths and gaps within simulation curricula, evaluate the impact of curricular interventions over time, guide resident-informed program improvements, and facilitate benchmarking across institutions.

articles.title: Factors Associated With Prolonged Emergency Department (ED) Length of Stay (LOS) at a Tertiary Care Hospital in Nepal: A Cross-Sectional Study.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Emergency department (ED) length of stay (LOS) is an important indicator of healthcare efficiency and patient flow. The duration of ED stay is influenced by a complex interaction of patient-related, clinical and system-level factors. Prolonged LOS (> 4 h) contributes to ED overcrowding and adverse patient outcomes. However, limited data exist regarding factors influencing ED LOS in Nepal.

abstract.label: METHOD
abstract.text: A descriptive cross-sectional study was conducted in the ED of KIST Medical College and Teaching Hospital (MCTH), a tertiary care hospital in Lalitpur, Nepal, from May 15, 2025, to May 30, 2025. All patients presenting to the ED during the study period were eligible for inclusion. Consecutive patient records were reviewed. ED LOS was defined as the time from patient arrival to ED exit. LOS was summarized using median and interquartile range (IQR). Group differences were assessed using the Mann-Whitney U and Kruskal-Wallis tests. Variables with p < 0.20 in univariate analysis were entered into a multivariable logistic regression model to identify factors independently associated with prolonged ED LOS (> 4 h). Adjusted odds ratios (aORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were reported.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 395 patients were included. The median ED LOS was 3.58 h (IQR 2.42-5.00). A total of 161 (40.8%) experienced prolonged ED LOS, while 234 (59.2%) had a LOS of ≤ 4 h. In univariate analysis, age, triage category, number of specialty consultations, payment method and requirement for advanced investigations were significantly associated with prolonged ED LOS (p < 0.05). On multivariable logistic regression analysis, increasing age, time of presentation and number of specialty consultations were independent predictors of prolonged ED LOS. Patients requiring single specialty consultation had higher odds of prolonged LOS (aOR 3.12; 95% CI 1.34-7.28), while those requiring multiple consultations had markedly higher odds (aOR 13.41; 95% CI 4.47-40.20). Presentation during night shift was associated with lower odds of prolonged LOS compared with morning shift (aOR 0.29; 95% CI 0.16-0.52).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: ED LOS in this tertiary care hospital was primarily influenced by patient age, time of presentation, consultation processes and administrative factors. Strengthening interdepartmental consultation processes and improving ED workflow efficiency may help reduce prolonged ED stay and overcrowding.

articles.title: Is Skeletal Maturity Associated With Anatomical Distribution of Sports-Related Lower Extremity Overuse Pain in Young Athletes?
articles.journal_full: Clinical journal of sport medicine : official journal of the Canadian Academy of Sport Medicine

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: To evaluate the association between skeletal maturity and the anatomical distribution of sports-related lower extremity overuse pain in young athletes.

abstract.label: DESIGN
abstract.text: Retrospective observational cohort study.

abstract.label: SETTING
abstract.text: Single-center sports medicine clinic.

abstract.label: PATIENTS/PARTICIPANTS
abstract.text: A total of 2565 clinical episodes of sports-related lower extremity overuse pain in athletes aged ≤22 years presenting between January 2017 and November 2025.

abstract.label: INDEPENDENT VARIABLES
abstract.text: Skeletal maturity classified according to physeal status (open vs closed).

abstract.label: MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES
abstract.text: Anatomical region of overuse pain at presentation. Anatomical distributions were compared between physeal groups, and multinomial logistic regression adjusted for sex and sport type evaluated associations between physeal status and anatomical presentation.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Overall anatomical distribution differed significantly according to skeletal maturity (P < 0.001). Although the knee was the most common anatomical region in both groups, athletes with open physes demonstrated relatively greater knee, pelvic girdle, and foot involvement, whereas athletes with closed physes demonstrated relatively greater ankle and lower-leg involvement. In adjusted multinomial logistic regression analyses, open physeal status was independently associated with a greater relative likelihood of foot (relative risk ratio [RRR], 2.65; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.95-3.61), knee (RRR, 2.45; 95% CI, 1.84-3.27), and pelvic girdle (RRR, 2.25; 95% CI, 1.59-3.20) presentations compared with ankle presentations. These associations remained consistent after additional adjustment for chronological age.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Skeletal maturity was associated with differences in anatomical distribution of sports-related lower extremity overuse pain. These findings suggest that skeletal maturity may influence where repetitive sport-related loading becomes clinically expressed and may improve the clinical interpretation of regional overuse pain in young athletes.

abstract.label: CLINICAL RELEVANCE
abstract.text: Considering skeletal maturity when evaluating regional overuse pain may improve the clinical interpretation of sports-related lower extremity pain in young athletes.

articles.title: Impact of on-site mobile CT imaging on prehospital patient management during the Munich Oktoberfest: a retrospective observational before-after study at a mass gathering.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Mass gatherings such as the Munich Oktoberfest increase demand on Emergency Medical Services (EMS), particularly for trauma patients requiring imaging. Suspected mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI) often necessitates hospital referral and diagnostic imaging, placing strain on prehospital and hospital resources.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This retrospective observational before-after study evaluated the impact of an on-site mobile computed tomography (CT) scanner deployed during the Oktoberfest in 2022 and 2023. Patients with suspected head, facial, or cervical spine trauma requiring CT imaging were included. EMS hospital transport data during these events (with mobile CT) were compared with a historical reference period from 2015 to 2019 (without mobile CT) and with matched pre- and post-event periods. Standardized prehospital protocols guided patient assessment and imaging decisions.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 498 patients underwent on-site CT imaging. Of these, 429 (86%) were treated on-site and discharged after imaging and clinical evaluation, while 52 (10%) required hospital transport based on CT findings. Additional transports occurred for unrelated medical issues. On-site CT availability prevented 429 EMS transports, corresponding to an estimated 22,737 min of EMS deployment time. Trauma-related hospital admissions during Oktoberfest were lower in 2022-2023 than in 2015-2019, and the relative increase in admissions during the event was reduced.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: This retrospective analysis of the use of a mobile CT scanner in a prehospital setting during a mass gathering found that its implementation was associated with improved patient triage, fewer hospital transports, and more efficient EMS resource utilization. While the retrospective before-after study design does not permit direct causal inference, on-site imaging may have contributed to more targeted patient management and reduced demand on hospital resources. These findings suggest that mobile CT could represent a useful model for supporting medical services at large-scale public events and warrant further prospective evaluation.

articles.title: DO Generations MAtter for Treatment of Outpatient Pyelonephritis With Cephalosporins in the Emergency Department? DOGMA-ED Study.

abstract.label: STUDY OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: The primary objective of this study was to compare the effectiveness between first-, second-, and third-generation oral cephalosporins for the treatment of pyelonephritis in adult patients discharged from the emergency department (ED).

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This was a multicenter, retrospective, observational cohort study of 11 geographically distributed academic US EDs. Patients aged ≥18 years who were diagnosed with pyelonephritis and discharged home on an oral cephalosporin from the ED between August 1, 2023 and January 1, 2025 were included. The primary outcome was treatment failure at 14 days between the cephalosporin generations. The composite outcome was defined as one of the following: (1) recurrence of symptoms, (2) repeat ED/urgent care visit due to urinary tract infection, (3) receipt of a new antibiotic prescription for urinary symptoms, or (4) hospitalization due to urinary tract infection. Secondary outcomes included the need to modify the patient's initial antimicrobial regimen based on culture and susceptibility.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 1,147 patients met inclusion, with 618 (53.9%) receiving a first-generation, 91 (7.9%) a second-generation, and 438 (38.2%) a third-generation cephalosporin. Baseline characteristics were similar across cohorts, with women comprising over 85% of the study population. The most prescribed agents were cephalexin (85% of first generation), cefuroxime (100% of second generation), and cefdinir (79% of third generation). There was no statistically significant difference in 14-day treatment failure rates across generations (first versus second: 19.6% versus 17.6%, difference 2.0%, 95% confidence interval (CI) -7.1 to 11.1; first versus third: 19.6% versus 18.0%, difference 1.6%, 95% CI -3.4 to 6.5).

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: First-, second-, and third-generation oral cephalosporins demonstrated comparable 14-day treatment failure rates for the treatment of acute pyelonephritis in patients discharged from the ED.

articles.title: From Model to Mastery: High-Fidelity Cricothyrotomy Simulation With a 3D-Printed and Biological Tissue Model.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: Emergency cricothyroidotomy is a rare procedure utilized in the setting of patients who cannot be oxygenated or intubated. To enhance training in this critical skill, we developed and validated an immersive, high-fidelity task trainer that integrates a 3D-printed airway model with a porcine soft-tissue layer, and we assessed its impact during simulation-based training sessions.

abstract.label: STUDY DESIGN
abstract.text: Observational.

abstract.label: SETTING
abstract.text: Single institution (16 otolaryngology and 30 emergency medicine trainees).

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Our trainer consisted of an accurate 3D-printed airway model and neck incorporating anatomical structures and a biological soft-tissue layer. A survey was administered before and after the simulation. The simulations were completed individually in a case-based scenario with vital signs monitors and supporting actors responding to the participant's management decisions. The participants debriefed with otolaryngology faculty. Differences among post graduate year were analyzed using analysis of variance (ANOVA) and two-tailed t tests.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Confidence regarding airway anatomy, management, and cricothyrotomy performance increased significantly after the simulation (P < .00001). Across all training levels, simulation elements such as adaptive vital signs and use of biological skin on the task trainer were rated highly, scoring an average of 8.7 and 9.7 out of 10, respectively. Participants rated the composite model, on average, 9.1 out of 10 on the post-simulation survey.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: High-quality simulation is essential for developing competence in cricothyrotomy, a procedure that is infrequent yet critical. The task trainer and simulation session described here provide a realistic, reproducible, and highly rated method for trainees to gain the skills and confidence necessary to perform emergent cricothyrotomy.

articles.title: Efficacy and Safety of Opioid Analgesia in Acute Abdominal Presentations: A Systematic Review.

abstract.text: Acute abdominal pain is a common emergency department presentation and is often associated with diagnostic uncertainty. Historically, opioid analgesia was used cautiously because of concern that it could alter physical examination findings and interfere with diagnostic accuracy. Non-opioid and opioid-sparing strategies are increasingly used for pain management. This systematic review evaluates the efficacy and safety of analgesic strategies for acute, non-traumatic abdominal pain, with attention to pain relief, adverse effects, rescue analgesia, and diagnostic accuracy. PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials were searched for randomized comparative trials of opioid-containing treatment versus non-opioid, opioid-sparing, or placebo strategies. Eligible studies included adults aged 18 years or older with acute abdominal pain or an acute intra-abdominal cause of pain; studies limited to renal or ureteric colic were excluded. Of the 316 records identified, 45 duplicates were removed, 271 records were screened, 26 reports underwent full-text assessment, and 16 randomized trials were included. Across the included trials, opioids provided effective short-term analgesia but were not consistently superior to alternatives. Hydromorphone produced greater pain improvement than intravenous lidocaine at 90 minutes (between-group difference = 1.2 points, 95% confidence interval (CI) = 0.3-2.2) with less rescue analgesia. In acute pancreatitis, median Visual Analog Scale (VAS) reductions at 30 minutes were 45.5 (95% CI = 30-54) with tramadol, 41.5 (95% CI = 34-50) with paracetamol, and 40.5 (95% CI = 30-47) with dexketoprofen, with no statistically significant between-group difference. An erector spinae plane block produced lower pain scores and reduced rescue fentanyl compared with intravenous tramadol. In biliary colic, mean pain relief at 30 minutes was 3.8 (95% CI = 2.4-5.2) with ketorolac and 3.9 (95% CI = 2.4-5.3) with meperidine, with no statistically significant between-group difference. Butorphanol provided greater early pain relief than ketorolac at 15 minutes but not at 30 minutes. Low-dose morphine plus paracetamol did not significantly differ from standard-dose morphine, and intravenous lidocaine and morphine did not significantly differ at the primary 60-minute endpoint. Several placebo-controlled trials assessed diagnostic accuracy using different definitions and patient populations. In one trial, diagnostic accuracy was 86% with morphine and 85% with placebo (difference 1 percentage point, 95% CI = -11 to 12). This imprecise estimate does not rule out a clinically important difference, and the available trials do not establish whether opioids affect diagnostic accuracy across acute abdominal presentations. Some studies identified changes in tenderness, rigidity, or localization after analgesia, but these were not consistently associated with diagnostic error or adverse management outcomes. Adverse effects were generally short-term and included nausea, vomiting, dizziness, and sedation, although most trials were not large enough or followed long enough to reliably evaluate uncommon serious adverse events. Overall, the evidence supports an individualized approach to analgesia. Opioids remain effective when clinically indicated, but are not consistently superior to non-opioid or opioid-sparing alternatives, and analgesia should not be routinely delayed solely because of concern for diagnostic interference.

articles.title: Minimally invasive versus open emergency right-sided colectomy for malignant obstruction: a nationwide propensity score-matched cohort study.
articles.journal_full: World journal of emergency surgery : WJES

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Minimally invasive surgery (MIS) improves short-term outcomes in elective colectomy, however, the choice of surgical approach in hemodynamically stable patients with obstructing right-sided colon cancer remains unclear in emergency settings. MIS could be considered and the present study aims to evaluate short-term outcomes of MIS in bowel obstructed patients compared with open surgery (OPEN).

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A retrospective nationwide study including patients from the nationwide Swedish Colorectal Cancer Registry (SCRCR) undergoing emergency right-sided colectomy in Sweden (2017-2023) was conducted. Propensity score matching (1:1) was performed based on sex, age, ASA class, hospital size, and operative timing (on-call vs. daytime). Outcomes included length of stay (LOS), postoperative complications, and surgical quality indicators. Analysis was performed according to intention-to-treat.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 1147 patients were identified. Of the 1,147 included patients, 99 (8.6%) underwent an initially minimally invasive approach. After matching, 99 patients remained in each group. The conversion rate was 34%. Median LOS was 9 days (IQR 6;14) after OPEN and 6 days (IQR 5;10) after MIS. In quantile regression with bootstrap standard errors, MIS was associated with a 3-day shorter median LOS (median difference - 3.0 days, 95% CI - 4 to - 2, p = 0.002). Postoperative complications (Clavien-Dindo ≥ 2) occurred in 38.8% after OPEN and in 23.2% after MIS. Logistic regression analysis with robust standard errors showed significantly lower odds of postoperative complications after MIS (OR 0.48, 95% CI 0.27-0.83, p = 0.009). No significant differences were observed in re-admission, 90-day mortality, R0 resection, lymph node yield, blood loss or operative time.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: In this nationwide observational cohort, an initially minimally invasive approach was associated with shorter length of stay and fewer postoperative complications. No statistically significant differences were observed in the available short-term surgical and pathological quality indicators. Given the limited number of MIS procedures and potential for residual confounding, these findings support further evaluation of MIS in carefully selected patients.

articles.title: Global Rate of Bystander Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation in Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) is a leading cause of mortality worldwide, and bystander cardiopulmonary resuscitation (BCPR) is one of determinants of survival. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to determine the prevalence of BCPR and investigate sources of heterogeneity.

abstract.label: METHOD
abstract.text: We conducted a systematic search of PubMed, Scopus, Embase, and Web of Science from inception until 1 August 2025, for observational studies that reported the incidence of BCPR in OHCA. We performed a random-effects meta-analysis to calculate the pooled prevalence of BCPR. Subgroup analyses were conducted to explore heterogeneity based on geography, income level, patient demographics, and study characteristics.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Our analysis included 229 studies encompassing 4,421,570 OHCA patients from 45 countries. The pooled prevalence of receiving BCPR was 32.1% (95% confidence interval [CI] 29.7%-34.5%), with substantial heterogeneity (I2=99.9%). BCPR rates were significantly higher in high-income countries compared to low- and middle-income countries (34.9% vs 13.9%; p<0.0001) and in paediatric versus adult populations (49.2% vs 31.4%; p=0.0002). OHCAs occurring in residential settings had a 28% lower likelihood of receiving BCPR than those in public locations (risk ratio [RR] 0.72; 95% CI 0.64-0.80). Furthermore, female patients were mildly less likely to receive BCPR than male patients (RR 0.96; 95% CI 0.93-0.99). Trend analysis revealed a modest but significant increase in BCPR prevalence over time (slope 0.29% per year; p=0.016).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Less than one-third of individuals with OHCA receive BCPR. Despite a modest temporal increase, significant and actionable disparities persist across income levels, geographic regions, patient populations, and arrest locations. These findings highlight the need for targeted public health interventions, policy reforms, and tailored educational strategies to address these inequities and improve the global response to OHCA.

articles.title: Towards automatic analysis of clinical notes for injuries of bicycles and other micromobility devices using natural language processing.
articles.journal_full: Injury prevention : journal of the International Society for Child and Adolescent Injury Prevention

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Micromobility-related injuries are increasing, yet injury surveillance systems lack comprehensive data on risk factors like helmet use. Unstructured clinical notes in electronic health records contain this valuable information, which is crucial for injury prevention efforts.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted a retrospective method comparison study comparing rule-based systems and machine learning models (Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency+eXtreme Gradient Boosting) for extracting helmet use information from emergency department triage notes. We analysed 1206 notes from micromobility-related injuries collected between 2018 and 2023 from three institutions: University of Washington Medicine facilities, Washington State Department of Health's Rapid Health Information NetwOrk system and the US Consumer Product Safety Commission's National Electronic Injury Surveillance System. Performance was evaluated using F1 score, precision and recall, with both internal and external validation (across three institutions) to assess generalisability.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: The rule-based system outperformed machine learning approaches, achieving F1 scores of 0.96 and 0.95 in two datasets and 0.86 in a third dataset, compared with machine learning models' F1 scores of approximately 0.80. The rule-based approach demonstrated higher precision and recall while requiring fewer computational resources. External validation confirmed the robustness of the rule-based system with minimal performance degradation across all three institutions.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: Despite the current emphasis on machine learning approaches for clinical text analysis, our findings indicate that rule-based systems remain effective for helmet use identification.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: For extraction tasks such as helmet use identification from triage notes, rule-based systems offer superior performance, reliability and efficiency compared with more complex machine learning models. These findings have implications for injury surveillance and prevention programme development.

articles.title: Transforming musculoskeletal injury management using Virtual Bones: a novel digital solution.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Managing musculoskeletal (MSK) injuries requires effective communication and collaboration between the emergency department (ED) and orthopaedic teams. A quality improvement project analysing virtual fracture clinic (VFC) referrals, staff challenges and the impact of the novel digital solution, Virtual Bones (VB), was undertaken at the West Suffolk Hospital. VB is a digital platform, available at the point of care, that guides clinicians in the assessment and management of MSK injury presentations in ED and referral to VFC.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: VFC outcome data were collected between 2017 and 2022, with a 2-week focused data collection gathering diagnosis, ED processing times, patient leaflet distribution, VFC decisions and referral quality. An ED survey was distributed to explore staff challenges in the management of MSK injuries. Virtual Bones, a novel digital solution, was developed and deployed to enable clinicians to comprehensively digitalise MSK injury management pathways from first patient encounter to referral/discharge. Subsequent data collection cycles compared baseline to post deployment results.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: The Virtual Bones pilot (undertaken May-July 2023) involved 352 users, 2400 sessions and 56 700 page views. The initial 2-week cycle included 260 patients while the subsequent cycles included a total of 258. Mean ED processing times decreased from 166 to 122 min, with an up to 90 min reduction in the Foundation Doctors' group (p<0.0001). Inappropriately referred dischargeable injuries decreased from 23 to 10. Improper documentation decreased from 58% to 30% (p<0.0001). The VFC discharge rate increased from 39% to 48% (p=0.021). Patient information leaflet use increased from 27% to 41% (p=0.032). The ED staff survey demonstrated improved staff confidence in the revealed challenges, including navigating local guidelines, locating equipment, applying immobilisation devices and supplying information leaflets.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Robust engagement with Virtual Bones, along with improved metrics, suggests that this digital solution effectively streamlined MSK injury pathways and helped staff manage challenges.

articles.title: Amiodarone after conversion from a non-shockable to a shockable rhythm in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: A propensity score-matched analysis from the German resuscitation registry.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Amiodarone should be administered after three shocks according the current ERC ALS guidelines. However, its effect in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) patients with an initial non-shockable rhythm who subsequently convert to a shockable rhythm is not established.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We performed a retrospective observational cohort study using data from the German Resuscitation Registry. Adult patients with non-traumatic OHCA, having an initial non-shockable rhythm and subsequently received at least two defibrillations were included. Propensity-score-matched patient pairs (1:1) were analysed to compare outcomes between patients who received amiodarone during resuscitation and those who did not. The primary outcome was survival to hospital discharge. Secondary outcomes included hospital admission with return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), 24-h survival, survival to hospital discharge, and favourable neurological outcome at hospital discharge.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Of 5535 patients included 3181 received amiodarone and 2354 did not. After propensity-score matching, 1843 patients remained in each group. Amiodarone administration was associated with higher rates of hospital admission with ROSC (26.7% vs. 23.0%; OR 1.22, 95% confidence interval 1.05-1.42), 24-h survival (21.4% vs. 14.7%; OR 1.58, 95% CI 1.33-1.87), and survival to hospital discharge (6.5% vs. 4.2%; OR 1.58, 95% CI 1.18-2.12). Favourable neurological outcome at hospital discharge was not statistically significant (3.7% vs. 2.9%; OR 1.31, 95% CI 0.91-1.89).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: In OHCA patients with an initial non-shockable rhythm who subsequently converted to a shockable rhythm, amiodarone administration was associated with improved short-term and long-term survival, but not with a statistically significant improved favourable neurological outcome. Future controlled studies might define the proper (earlier) time of amiodarone administration.

articles.title: Impact of cardiac rhythm dynamics during cardiopulmonary resuscitation on clinical outcomes in patients treated with extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR): a systematic review and meta-analysis.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Although the initial presenting cardiac rhythm is an established prognostic factor for extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation, heart rhythm dynamics during conventional cardiopulmonary resuscitation remain poorly studied. We evaluated how the evolution of rhythm affects neurological outcomes and survival among recipients of extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We systematically searched PubMed and Embase for studies evaluating rhythm dynamics, focusing on Rhythm Improvement (from non-shockable to shockable) or Rhythm Decay (from shockable to non-shockable). The primary outcome was survival with a favorable neurological outcome at the longest follow-up; the secondary outcome was overall survival. A random-effects model analysis with the Hartung-Knapp adjustment was used.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Ten observational studies evaluating 5183 subjects with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest treated with extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation were included. Rhythm improvement was associated with a higher probability of a favorable neurological outcome (RR 3.12, 95% CI 1.26-7.74; GRADE: Low) compared with refractory non-shockable rhythms. Conversely, rhythm decay reduced the likelihood of a favorable neurological outcome compared with a sustained shockable rhythm (RR 0.41, 95% CI 0.21-0.80; GRADE: Moderate). Notably, decay toward asystole showed a robust negative association with good neurological recovery (RR 0.20, 95% CI 0.09-0.45; GRADE: Moderate), whereas decay toward pulseless electrical activity did not reach statistical significance (RR 0.62, 95% CI 0.31-1.25; GRADE: Low).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Rhythm dynamics provide valuable prognostic insights for candidates for extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation. Rhythm decay toward asystole may predict resuscitation failure and poor neurological survival, suggesting that it should prompt a critical re-evaluation of the appropriateness of extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation.

articles.title: Non-enrolment and non-completion of cardiac rehabilitation among survivors of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest with ischaemic aetiology: a nationwide register-based cohort study.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) of ischaemic aetiology is increasing, yet access to and completion of cardiac rehabilitation remain uncertain.

abstract.label: AIM
abstract.text: To investigate non-enrolment in and non-completion of cardiac rehabilitation among OHCA survivors of ischaemic aetiology including temporal trends, and to examine sociodemographic characteristics associated with non-participation and non-completion.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This nationwide Danish register-based cohort study included adults surviving ≥30 days after a first-time OHCA between 2019 and 2023. Multivariable logistic regression models were used to examine the association between non-enrolment and non-completion, respectively, and sociodemographic parameters of age, sex, cohabitation, comorbidity, education, and employment.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 1684 OHCA survivors were included. Overall, 55% did not enrol in CR, and among those who enrolled, 50% did not complete the programme. Non-enrolment was highest in 2020-2022 (60-62%) and declined to 43% in 2023. Survivors who were retired had higher odds of non-enrolment (OR 1.74, 95% CI 1.42-2.44), whereas higher education (OR 0.76, 95% CI 0.55-0.98) and moderate/severe comorbidity (OR 0.53, 95% CI 0.43-0.65) were associated with lower odds of non-enrolment. No sociodemographic characteristics were significantly associated with non-completion.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: A large proportion of OHCA survivors of ischaemic aetiology either did not enrol in or did not complete cardiac rehabilitation. The findings underscore the need for systematic referral to cardiac rehabilitation after OHCA and more tailored rehabilitation approaches.

articles.title: Most older long-term care residents in Oslo have documented do-not-resuscitate status: a cross-sectional study.

abstract.text: With population aging, understanding the frequency and distribution of decisions to attempt or withhold cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) in long-term care populations is increasingly important. In Oslo, CPR status, that is, an advance decision about whether CPR should or should not be attempted, is systematically assessed and documented for all long-term care residents. Comprehensive register data therefore provide a unique opportunity to assess advance CPR decisions at the population level. We obtained cross-sectional data on the documented CPR status of nearly all persons aged 50+ years admitted to public or private long-term care facilities in Oslo between 2018 and 2023 (N = 7860). We examined the proportion of long-term care residents with documented positive CPR status (CPR should be attempted) and used multivariable logistic regression to analyze the associations between documented positive CPR status and age, sex, marital status, primary contact (e.g., son, daughter, spouse, professional), functional limitations, institutional relocations, duration of stay, and year of admission. We found that 9.2% of long-term care residents had documented positive CPR status. Documented positive CPR status was related to younger age, fewer limitations, shorter duration of stay, and fewer relocations. Compared with residents first admitted in 2018, documented positive CPR status was less likely among those first admitted between 2019 and 2022, but not among those first admitted in 2023. There was no evidence that documented positive CPR status was related to sex, marital status, primary contact. Our findings provide population-level evidence on documented CPR status in long-term care and highlight the need for future research on how such decisions are made.

articles.title: Time to return of spontaneous circulation and long-term outcomes in bystander-witnessed out-of-hospital cardiac arrest survivors.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND AND AIMS
abstract.text: Immediate Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) survival is time-sensitive, however, evidence linking resuscitation time to recovery is limited. We examined time from emergency call to return of spontaneous circulation (time-to-ROSC) and survivor outcomes.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: From the Danish Cardiac Arrest Registry, we included adults with bystander-witnessed OHCA (2016-2023) surviving ≥30 days, without prior anoxic brain damage or nursing home admission. Time-to-event and multivariable regression analyses stratified by time-to-ROSC (A: 0-10, B: 11-18, C: >18 min) assessed 11-month anoxic brain damage and nursing home admission, plus long-term survival and return-to-work through December 2024.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: We included 2583 patients (n = 875, 869, 839; groups A-C, respectively), 78% male; median age 65; median time-to-ROSC 14 min. Anoxic brain damage increased with time-to-ROSC (A-C: 0.3%, 1.8%, 3.2%; p < 0.001). Adjusted analyses showed an overall association (p = 0.03); HRs: 5.58 (95% CI 1.58-19.64) for B and 9.98 (95% CI 2.93-33.96) for C versus A. Nursing home admission decreased with time-to-ROSC (A-C: 3.1%, 2.2%, 1.3%; p = 0.04), but adjustments attenuated the association (p = 0.3). Long-term survival was similar (5-year Kaplan-Meier estimate: 79%; 95% CI 77-81%; p = 0.80; adjusted p = 0.99). Among employed patients (n = 177, 168, 179), return-to-work was similar (5-year cumulative incidence: 60%; 95% CI 56-65%; p = 0.31; adjusted p = 0.29).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: In bystander-witnessed 30-day OHCA survivors, prolonged resuscitation does not preclude recovery, time-to-ROSC was associated with anoxic brain damage but not nursing home admission, return-to-work, or long-term survival.

articles.title: Automated external defibrillators for in-hospital cardiac arrest: a systematic review.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Automated external defibrillators (AEDs) improve survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, but their role in in-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA) remains uncertain. This systematic review evaluates whether ward-accessible AED capability prior to code blue team arrival improves survival and neurologic outcomes compared with standard resuscitation systems.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Six databases were searched. Eligible studies compared AED use to manual defibrillation in IHCA outside specialized areas. Primary outcome was survival with favorable neurological status (CPC 1-2, mRS 0-3, or no deterioration from baseline). Secondary outcomes included ROSC, survival at 24 h, survival to discharge, 30-day survival, CPR quality, and timing metrics. Three independent reviewers performed study selection, data extraction, and risk-of-bias assessment. Due to substantial heterogeneity, results were synthesized descriptively.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Six reports from five unique study cohorts met inclusion criteria (total screened = 5510). Neurologically favorable survival was inconsistent. One study reported improved outcomes following a combined AED-and-training intervention, whereas the largest multicentre cohort found no significant difference in neurological disability among survivors (adjusted relative risk 1.01, 95% CI 0.93-1.09). ROSC and survival to discharge were not consistently improved. Only one study directly quantified AED-associated compression pauses, and effects on time to defibrillation varied by setting.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Available evidence is insufficient to determine whether routine ward-level AED deployment improves IHCA outcomes. Included studies were observational and heterogeneous and CPR quality and training were incompletely characterized. Potential benefit from earlier defibrillation in shockable rhythms must be weighed against possible compression interruptions. Contemporary comparative studies are needed.

articles.title: Prehospital prognostication after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest in tertiary care centers: the R-EDByUS score in the JAAM-OHCA registry.

abstract.label: AIM
abstract.text: The R-EDByUS score predicts unfavorable neurological outcomes after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) using prehospital variables alone, with separate models based on return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) status at hospital arrival. However, whether the score remains valid in patients transported to tertiary care centers is uncertain. We therefore aimed to validate it externally in this setting.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Using the JAAM-OHCA Registry, we analyzed adult patients with presumed cardiogenic OHCA transported to tertiary care centers. The regression-based R-EDByUS score was applied to predict unfavorable neurological outcome (Cerebral Performance Category 3-5) at 1 month in the prehospital ROSC and ongoing cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) cohorts. Discrimination and calibration were assessed, and score performance was examined across in-hospital intervention subgroups (percutaneous coronary intervention, targeted temperature management, and extracorporeal membrane oxygenation). We also assessed the proportion of patients with unfavorable outcomes among those with a predicted probability ≥99%.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Of 29,345 patients, 3305 were classified into the prehospital ROSC cohort and 26,040 into the ongoing CPR cohort. The score showed good discrimination, with areas under the curve of 0.906 and 0.913, and good calibration in the prehospital ROSC cohort. Discrimination was lower among patients who received PCI, TTM, or ECMO in the ongoing CPR cohort. Among patients with a predicted probability ≥99%, 100% (112/112; prehospital ROSC) and 99.9% (20,560/20,588; ongoing CPR) had unfavorable outcomes.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: The R-EDByUS score showed good discrimination in the JAAM-OHCA Registry, supporting its use for early risk stratification in cardiogenic OHCA even in tertiary care centers.

articles.title: Design and rationale of the TANGO2 trial: A randomized controlled non-inferiority trial of bystander compression-only CPR versus standard CPR in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.

abstract.label: RATIONALE
abstract.text: Bystander cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) before emergency medical services arrival is associated with improved survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA). Compression-only CPR (COCPR) is simpler to teach and perform, eliminates interruptions in chest compressions for rescue breaths, and has been associated with higher bystander CPR rates. For adults with OHCA of presumed medical etiology, clinical equipoise remains regarding the optimal CPR strategy for previously trained bystanders.

abstract.label: PRIMARY HYPOTHESIS
abstract.text: Bystander COCPR is non-inferior to standard CPR (S-CPR) for 30-day survival in dispatch-assisted out-of-hospital cardiac arrest DESIGN: TANGO2 is an international, multicenter, randomized, open-label, non-inferior trial. Dispatchers randomize eligible cases 1:1 to COCPR or S-CPR via an integrated decision-support system. Protocol adherence is evaluated via systematic dispatch audio review. Per-protocol (PP) analysis is prespecified as the primary analysis, supported by modified intention-to-treat (mITT) analysis. Non-inferiority is defined as an absolute risk difference above -1.0 percentage points.

abstract.label: SITES
abstract.text: All Emergency Medical Dispatch Centers in Sweden and selected sites in Italy.

abstract.label: ESTIMATED ENROLLMENT
abstract.text: A total of 3,260 per-protocol EMS-treated OHCA patients ENROLLMENT DATES: Start date: 2017. Estimated completion date: December 2027.

abstract.label: CURRENT STATUS
abstract.text: Enrolling.

abstract.label: TRIAL REGISTRATION
abstract.text: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT03981107, https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03981107.

articles.title: Utilisation of poison information services for paediatric snakebites in rural Sri Lanka.
articles.journal_full: Toxicon : official journal of the International Society on Toxinology

abstract.text: Paediatric snakebites can present substantial diagnostic and therapeutic uncertainty, particularly in rural hospitals where access to specialist toxicology expertise may be limited. Emergency expert advice services may support frontline clinicians, but their utilisation and perceived value remain poorly understood. We conducted a qualitative study among 42 physicians working in four hospitals serving snakebite-endemic regions of Sri Lanka. Eight focus group discussions were conducted at Teaching Hospital Batticaloa, District General Hospital Polonnaruwa, District General Hospital Trincomalee and Teaching Hospital Kurunegala. A semi-structured guide explored circumstances prompting consultation, clinical decision-making, reasons for non-utilisation, perceived benefits, barriers to access and priorities for service improvement. Discussions were audio-recorded, transcribed and analysed thematically using Braun and Clarke's framework. Six interrelated themes were identified. Expert advice was primarily sought in the context of clinical uncertainty, unidentified snakes, severe envenoming, antivenom decisions and complications. Advice was perceived to support critical management decisions, provide reassurance and increase clinicians' confidence, with potential benefits for patient management and avoidance of unnecessary treatment. Utilisation was moderated by the availability of consultants and senior colleagues, with external advice less frequently sought for straightforward cases or when local expertise was readily accessible. Important barriers included limited availability, particularly at night, busy telephone lines, connectivity problems, delayed responses and difficulty identifying the correct contact number. Participants advocated 24-h and island-wide access, improved communication pathways, regular training, point-of-care educational resources and digital platforms. Expert advice services provide an important layer of specialist decision support for physicians managing paediatric snakebites. Improving accessibility while integrating expert consultation with training, clinical guidance and digital decision-support tools may strengthen snakebite care in rural settings.

articles.title: Disaster preparedness perceptions and associated factors among final-year medical students in Hatay and Ordu, Türkiye.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Following the February 2023 Türkiye earthquakes, disaster preparedness among healthcare professionals and medical students has become an important public health concern, particularly in disaster-prone settings where newly graduated physicians may be rapidly deployed to frontline healthcare services. However, evidence on disaster preparedness perceptions among medical students remains limited, especially in comparative settings involving regions with different levels of disaster exposure. This study aimed to assess disaster preparedness perception and associated factors among final-year medical students studying in two provinces of Türkiye with differing disaster risk profiles in the aftermath of the February 2023 earthquakes.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A cross-sectional study was conducted between April and May 2023 among final-year medical students from Hatay Mustafa Kemal University and Ordu University, Türkiye. Data were collected through a structured self-administered online questionnaire covering sociodemographic and disaster-related characteristics, an author-developed earthquake healthcare knowledge test, and the Disaster Preparedness Perception Scale of Personnel Working in Pre-Hospital Emergency Health Services (HASPAHA). Univariable analyses and multivariable logistic regression were performed to identify factors independently associated with high perceived preparedness, which was defined using a median split.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 188 students participated (109 in Hatay, 79 in Ordu). The mean disaster preparedness perception score was 101.5 ± 13.6 (scale range: 28-140), with significantly higher scores observed in Hatay compared to Ordu. In multivariable analysis, male sex (aOR=3.13) and studying in Hatay (aOR=2.11) were associated with high perceived preparedness. Willingness to volunteer in disaster healthcare services (aOR=3.99) and higher earthquake healthcare knowledge (aOR=2.95) were also significant associated factors.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Among final-year medical students, perceived preparedness was associated with regional disaster exposure context and motivational characteristics, alongside earthquake healthcare knowledge. To strengthen future physicians' preparedness, medical curricula could incorporate experiential disaster training, opportunities for voluntary participation in disaster response, and structured disaster preparedness education.

articles.title: Relative Roles of Middle Ear Bulla Volume and Eustachian Tube Function in Diving-related Barotrauma: An Experimental Pressure Chamber Study in Guinea Pigs.
articles.journal_full: Otology & neurotology : official publication of the American Otological Society, American Neurotology Society [and] European Academy of Otology and Neurotology

abstract.label: HYPOTHESIS
abstract.text: We hypothesized that isolated changes in middle ear air volume do not increase the risk of diving-related middle ear barotrauma, and that Eustachian tube function is the primary determinant of barotrauma development.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: The relative contributions of middle ear air volume and Eustachian tube function to the development of diving-related middle ear barotrauma remain controversial. This first experimental comparative study aimed to differentiate the effects of middle ear air volume alteration and Eustachian tube function on barotrauma in guinea pigs exposed to high pressure.

abstract.label: MATERIALS AND METHODS
abstract.text: A diving protocol using a pressure chamber was applied to 18 guinea pigs with normal hearing and otoscopic findings (first dive simulation). Ears developing barotrauma were recorded. Three weeks later, after complete recovery was confirmed, bulla obliteration was performed in the left ears of 12 randomly selected guinea pigs (obliteration group), while the right ears underwent bulla opening without obliteration (sham surgery group). After a 2-week wound-healing period, the same diving protocol was repeated (second dive simulation). Otoscopic examination, tympanometry, and auditory brainstem response measurements were then performed, followed by decapitation. In a double-blind design, botulinum toxin was injected into the Eustachian tube muscles on one side of the remaining 6 guinea pigs (botox group), and physiological saline was injected on the contralateral side (saline control group).

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Some degree of barotrauma was commonly seen in all ears. Within-group comparisons of barotrauma occurrence after the first and second dive simulations showed no significant differences in the obliteration, sham, or saline groups. In contrast, barotrauma developed in all ears in which the Eustachian tube muscles were paralyzed with botulinum toxin.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Isolated reduction of middle ear volume by bulla obliteration did not influence the development of diving-related middle ear barotrauma. In contrast, functional blockade of the Eustachian tube resulted in consistent barotrauma, indicating that Eustachian tube function is the primary determinant of susceptibility to barotrauma during acute pressure changes. Middle ear volume may, therefore, be better interpreted as a long-term marker of Eustachian tube function rather than a direct causal factor.

articles.title: Adjunctive hyperbaric oxygen therapy in high-risk oculoplastic reconstructions requiring graft-based surgery: a retrospective case series.

abstract.label: PURPOSE
abstract.text: To evaluate the postoperative healing course and clinical outcomes of high-risk oculoplastic reconstructions requiring graft-based surgery, in which adjunctive hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) was used to support wound healing.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This retrospective case series included 11 patients who underwent oculoplastic surgery with graft-based reconstruction and were considered at high risk for delayed healing and/or tissue compromise. Indications for surgery were orbital implant (sphere) exposure repair (n = 5), cicatricial entropion (n = 1), necrotizing scleritis (n = 1), tissue loss following trauma (n = 1), wound dehiscence and infection after lower eyelid blepharoplasty (n = 1), orbital cellulitis following endophthalmitis and evisceration after cataract surgery (n = 1), and delayed wound healing after dermolipoma excision (n = 1). All patients received graft-based surgical management with adjunctive HBOT. Demographic data, culture results, number of HBOT sessions, and recovery time were analyzed. Patients were evaluated according to HBOT exposure (10 vs. 20 sessions).

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: All patients underwent graft-supported surgical repair in the setting of anticipated difficult healing. Culture growth was detected in 5 patients. Clinical stabilization and wound closure were achieved without the need for additional major reconstructive procedures in most cases. Patients receiving 20 HBOT sessions had a longer observed mean recovery time compared with those receiving 10 sessions (82.6 vs. 40.9 days; p = 0.032).

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: In a heterogeneous cohort of high-risk oculoplastic reconstructions requiring grafting-including orbital implant exposure repair and complex inflammatory, infectious, or traumatic etiologies-adjunctive HBOT was used as a supportive modality and was associated with acceptable healing outcomes. The longer recovery observed with extended (20-session) HBOT courses likely reflects greater baseline disease severity rather than a reduced treatment effect. Given the retrospective design and clinical heterogeneity, further studies are needed to clarify patient selection criteria and define optimal HBOT protocols in oculoplastic reconstruction.
