abstract.text: This retrospective diagnostic accuracy study included 200 POCUS cases from four hospitals (two in Israel and two in the United States). Each case was independently interpreted by three cardiologists and the device for seven measurements [left ventricular (LV) ejection fraction, inferior vena cava (IVC) maximal diameter, left atrial (LA) area, right atrial (RA) area, LV end-diastolic diameter, right ventricular (RV) fractional area change, and aortic root diameter]. The endpoints were the root mean square error (RMSE) of the device compared with the average cardiologist measurement (LV ejection fraction and IVC maximal diameter were primary endpoints; the other measurements were secondary endpoints). Predefined passing criteria were based on the upper bounds of the RMSE 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The intercardiologist RMSE was also calculated for reference.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: The device achieved the passing criteria for six of the seven measurements. Although not achieving the passing criterion for RV fractional area change, it still achieved a better RMSE than the intercardiologist RMSE. The RMSE was 6.20% [95% confidence interval (CI): 5.57-6.83; intercardiologist RMSE of 8.23%] for LV ejection fraction, 0.25 cm (95% CI: 0.20-0.29; 0.36 cm) for IVC maximal diameter, 2.39 cm2 (95% CI: 1.96-2.82; 4.39 cm2) for LA area, 2.11 cm2 (95% CI: 1.75-2.47; 3.49 cm2) for RA area, 5.06 mm (95% CI: 4.58-5.55; 4.67 mm) for LV end-diastolic diameter, 10.17% (95% CI: 9.01-11.33; 14.12%) for RV fractional area change, and 0.19 cm (95% CI: 0.16-0.21; 0.24 cm) for aortic root diameter.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: The device accurately calculated these cardiac measurements especially when benchmarked against intercardiologist variability. Its use could assist clinicians who utilize POCUS and better enable their clinical decision-making.

articles.title: Hidden burden of pneumococcal colonization in adults with viral respiratory infections: the role of influenza and RSV.
articles.journal_full: Frontiers in cellular and infection microbiology

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Although pneumococcal colonization is uncommon in adults, it may increase during respiratory viral infections. We investigated the frequency of pneumococcal colonization, associated factors, and serotype distribution in adults with confirmed respiratory viral infection.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We prospectively included adults presenting to the Emergency Department of Bellvitge University Hospital with influenza A virus (IAV), SARS-CoV-2, or respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection, as well as 33 virus-negative controls (December 2023-January 2024). Nasopharyngeal swabs were tested for Streptococcus pneumoniae using a RT-PCR assay (lytA and piaB genes). Clinical data were analysed using Cox proportional hazards regression models.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 616 episodes were studied (IAV, n=391; SARS-CoV-2, n=162; RSV, n=28; >1 virus, n=35). Pneumococcal colonization was detected in 85 individuals, with the highest prevalence among IAV-infected patients (14.8%), followed by RSV (10.7%) and SARS-CoV-2 (9.3%). Individuals with viral infection showed higher pneumococcal loads (median lytA CT 23.1 [18.7-27.4]) compared to those without infection (CT 31.8 [31.5-33.3]). IAV (OR 3.52; 95%CI 1.30-9.17) and RSV (OR 4.04; 95%CI 1.11-13.50) were independently associated with pneumococcal colonization. Among adults <65 years, female sex (OR for male sex 0.43; 95% CI 0.19-0.90) was associated with colonization, whereas in those ≥65 years, RSV infection (OR 5.56; 95% CI 1.03-27.31) was the main association. Detected serotypes were diverse, predominantly non-PCV serotypes.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Pneumococcal colonization was more frequent during IAV or RSV than SARS-CoV-2 infection. In older adults, RSV infection showed a particularly strong association, highlighting potential implications for pneumococcal and RSV vaccination strategies.

articles.title: Recent Advances in Adiabatic Compressed Air Energy Storage Systems with Thermal Energy Storage: Classification and Control Strategies.

abstract.text: Driven by accelerating global electrification and the increasing share of renewable energy, adiabatic compressed air energy storage (ACAES) has emerged as a promising long-duration energy storage solution for grid-scale applications. The successful development of 300 MW class demonstration projects further indicates the growing commercial potential of ACAES with round-trip efficiencies exceeding 70%. This paper provides a comprehensive review of the system classification, thermal energy storage (TES), compressed air reservoirs (CARs), and cutting-edge control strategies of the ACAES systems. Distinct from previous reviews focused on individual technologies, this review establishes a multilevel, design-oriented perspective spanning component selection, system configuration, operational control, and grid-level dispatch, thereby integrating fragmented technological knowledge to systematic guidance for the design, optimization, and operation of ACAES systems. First, the characteristics and performances of low-temperature (LT-ACAES), medium-temperature (MT-ACAES), and high-temperature ACAESs (HT-ACAES) are systematically compared. Although HT-ACAES can achieve the highest round-trip efficiency, up to 80.2%, its commercialization is constrained by high material costs and long-term reliability challenges, whereas LT-ACAES is limited by thermodynamic performance limits. MT-ACAES therefore represents a favorable compromise among efficiency, cost, and technological maturity, making it a promising candidate for near-term deployment. Current studies further demonstrate that overall ACAES performance is governed strongly by system-level configuration, highlighting the importance of multistage compression and expansion, optimized heat-exchanger networks, advanced TES configurations, and reduced throttling losses. For TES, the selection of liquid and solid media is strongly temperature dependent. Water is preferable for low-temperature applications, thermal oil is more suitable for medium-temperature systems, and molten salts become advantageous at higher temperatures, while low-cost natural rocks and concrete are attractive for large-scale sensible heat storage, and metal oxides show greater potential under ultra-high-temperature conditions. For CARs, salt caverns remain the preferred choice for large-scale and long-duration applications where suitable geology exists, whereas lined rock caverns, abandoned mines, depleted gas reservoirs, abandoned oil wells, and above-ground pressure vessels provide alternatives for different geological and deployment conditions. Reservoir performance is further governed by coupled thermodynamic, mechanical, seepage, and interfacial degradation processes, which jointly determine the airtightness, structural integrity, and long-term reliability. Control strategies are subsequently reviewed across charging and discharging regulation, mode switching, and system dispatch. Their development has progressed from single-objective and rule-based control toward coordinated multiobjective regulation, transient disturbance suppression, model predictive control, machine learning-assisted optimization, and security-constrained dispatch, enabling simultaneous improvements in round-trip efficiency, dynamic response, operational safety, and grid-support capability. Finally, key research gaps are identified in high-temperature material durability, long-term multiphysics reservoir modeling, integrated turbomachinery-TES dynamics, multitime scale dispatch-control coordination, and fault-tolerant operation under extreme grid disturbances. By integrating thermodynamic design, TES material selection, CAR behavior, and advanced control strategies, this review provides systematic guidance for the design, optimization, and reliable deployment of next-generation ACAES systems.

articles.title: Application of procalcitonin in pediatric emergency and critical care settings.

abstract.text: This expert consensus on the clinical application of procalcitonin (PCT) in pediatric emergency and critical care was convened by the Taiwan Society of Pediatric Emergency Medicine (TSPEM) and formulated by a committee of 14 leading experts. In pediatric emergency and critical care medicine, distinguishing between bacterial and viral etiologies remains a significant challenge, as clinical symptoms often lack specificity. While traditional biomarkers such as white blood cell count (WBC) and Creactive protein (CRP) provide reference values, they possess limitations regarding diagnostic timeliness and accuracy. In contrast, PCT serves as a specific biomarker for bacterial infections with superior kinetic advantages, rising rapidly within 3 to 6 hours of infection. It demonstrates greater sensitivity than CRP in the early detection of bacterial infections and in reflecting disease severity. This consensus recommends PCT as a vital adjunctive diagnostic tool, particularly for the early diagnosis and risk stratification of lower respiratory tract infections, bacterial meningitis, and sepsis. Specifically within the Pediatric Intensive Care Unit (PICU), PCT levels are valuable for monitoring disease progression and assessing the risk of sepsis-associated organ dysfunction. Furthermore, PCT plays a pivotal role in antimicrobial stewardship by providing objective guidance for the initiation and deescalation of antibiotic therapy, thereby effectively reducing unnecessary antibiotic exposure and mitigating the risk of antimicrobial resistance. Although PCT entails higher costs, studies indicate that its combination with CRP enhances diagnostic value. The committee emphasizes that PCT should be utilized as an "adjunctive aid" rather than a sole determinant of clinical decision-making. Clinicians must integrate PCT results with the patient's overall clinical presentation and employ dynamic serial monitoring to optimize care quality and therapeutic outcomes in pediatric emergency and critical care settings.

articles.title: Evaluation of University Undergraduate Students' Knowledge and Competency Following a First Responder's Training in Nigeria.
articles.journal_full: Journal of the West African College of Surgeons

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Emergency medical services for injured patients are grossly deficient in many parts of the low- and middle-income countries, including Nigeria. This allows the initial stabilisation and transportation of the injured to be done by untrained laypersons. This study sought to evaluate the effects of first responder training among university undergraduates in Nigeria.

abstract.label: MATERIALS AND METHODS
abstract.text: A 1-day first responder course was conducted for university undergraduates in Ilorin, Nigeria. Pretest and post-test were performed to measure first aid knowledge improvement and improved confidence in providing first aid care.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 127 university undergraduates (56.7% female), whose median age was 21 years, completed the training. About 61% of the trainees had no previous exposure to first aid training. The mean knowledge score improved from 40.2% before the training to 66.5% after the training (P < 0.0001). The results demonstrated significant improvement in most areas of first aid knowledge assessed. The greatest increase in knowledge was observed for bleeding control. There was also an increase in the mean skill confidence score from 2.77 to 4.69 (P = 0.01).

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: This study has shown that basic first responder training improves students' knowledge and perceived skill confidence in the provision of first aid care. Further research is underway to assess knowledge retention and skill utilisation during follow-up.

articles.title: Predictors of Pre-hospital Delay in Myocardial Infarction: A Cross-sectional Study at a Tertiary Care Center of Ahmedabad, India.
articles.journal_full: Indian journal of community medicine : official publication of Indian Association of Preventive & Social Medicine

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Myocardial infarction (MI) is a leading cause of death globally, with early treatment being critical in reducing mortality. Understanding determinants contributing to pre-hospital delay is essential to improve the outcome.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: The present study evaluated the time distribution between symptom onsets to hospital arrival and associated factors among patients with MI.

abstract.label: MATERIALS AND METHODS
abstract.text: A cross-sectional study included 105 MI patients admitted to a tertiary care teaching hospital in Ahmedabad city during March to August 2024. Patients fulfilling the inclusion criteria were interviewed using a pre-tested, semi-structured questionnaire. Pre-hospital delay was considered as the time elapsed from symptom onset to arrival at a tertiary care hospital among MI patients. Delay was categorized into two groups: ≤2 hours and >2 hours. Appropriate statistical tests were used to assess the association between factors influencing the time from symptom onset to hospital arrival.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: The median time from symptom onset to tertiary hospital arrival was 90 minutes (Interquartile range: 45-210 minutes). Out of a total of 105 participants, 37 (35.2%) experienced delays of >2 hours. Younger age (odds ratio [OR]: 2.16; P = 0.171), female gender (OR: 3.2; P = 0.03), and nuclear family structure (OR: 1.56; P = 0.39) were predictors of pre-hospital delay. Patients having previous similar episodes of symptoms or who misinterpreted them as non-heart-related also reported longer delays.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Approximately one-third of patients reported a delay of >2 hours. Younger age, female gender, nuclear family structure, previous episodes of symptoms, and misinterpretation of symptoms were significant determinants of pre-hospital delay in MI patients.

articles.title: Low-dose, high-frequency simulation with respiratory function monitor feedback enhances face mask ventilation across neonatal resuscitation devices: A prospective study in neonatology fellows.

abstract.text: Face mask ventilation (FMV) is a critical skill in neonatal resuscitation, yet structured assessment of neonatology fellow competence has remained limited. This study evaluated whether low-dose, high-frequency simulation with real-time respiratory function monitor (RFM) feedback improved FMV performance across commonly used ventilation devices. A prospective, single-center study was conducted over nine months involving neonatology fellows who performed simulated FMV using a T-piece resuscitator, self-inflating bag, and flow-inflating bag. Each session included blinded and unblinded RFM conditions. Primary outcomes included tidal volume (TV) within target range, mask leak, peak inspiratory pressure (PIP), positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP), respiratory rate, and self-reported proficiency. Mixed-effects models accounted for repeated measures. TV within goal range was higher with RFM feedback (80.3% vs 62.3%, p < 0.0001) and mask leak was lower with feedback across all three devices. No independent effect of feedback was observed for PIP or respiratory rate. Increasing session number improved respiratory rate, PIP, and PEEP but did not significantly improve TV or mask leak, suggesting limited skill improvement without feedback. Performance varied by device modestly, but higher performance was associated with RFM feedback and practice sessions across all devices. Self-reported confidence improved significantly across all devices, though clinical FMV frequency did not change. These findings support the use of RFMs in neonatal training regardless of device type while highlighting the need for strategies to improve long-term skill retention.

articles.title: Serial plasma proenkephalin A 119-159 and dipeptidyl peptidase 3 after cardiac arrest: association with long-term neurological outcome.

abstract.label: UNLABELLED
abstract.text: To evaluate whether serial plasma proenkephalin A 119-159 (penKid) and circulating dipeptidyl peptidase 3 (cDPP3) after cardiac arrest are associated with long-term neurological outcome and mortality.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We performed a retrospective multicentre cohort study of adults admitted to intensive care after cardiac arrest in southern Sweden. Biomarkers were measured on admission and at 12 and 48 h. The primary outcome was poor neurological outcome, defined as Cerebral Performance Category 3-5 at 2-6 months. The secondary outcome was 180-day mortality. Models were adjusted for established peri-arrest prognostic variables. Odds ratios and hazard ratios are reported per 1-SD increase in log10transformed biomarker concentration.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Among 417 patients, 271 (65%) had poor neurological outcome and 266 (64%) died within 180 days. PenKid was independently associated with poor neurological outcome at admission (adjusted odds ratio 1.62, 95% confidence interval 1.15-2.28) and 12 h (1.50, 1.08-2.09), and with mortality at admission (adjusted hazard ratio 1.36, 1.20-1.54) and 12 h (1.33, 1.17-1.51). cDPP3 was independently associated with mortality at 12 h (1.26, 1.11-1.43), but not with poor neurological outcome after adjustment. Neither biomarker significantly improved discrimination beyond the clinical reference model.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Early penKid was associated with poor neurological outcome and mortality after cardiac arrest, whereas cDPP3 was associated with mortality at 12 h. These biomarkers added limited discriminatory value beyond established clinical predictors.

articles.title: Evaluation of adherence to national regulations for documentation of limitations of life-sustaining treatments after a limited intervention at a Swedish hospital.

abstract.label: AIM
abstract.text: The aim of this study was to improve adherence to the Swedish National Board of Health and Welfare's regulations for documenting decisions regarding Limitations of Life-Sustaining Treatments at Capio St. Göran's Hospital in Stockholm following a limited intervention.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This was a before-and-after-study. The intervention took place in June 2023 and consisted of three parts: 1. Implementation of a modified digital medical record form for documentation of decisions regarding limitations of Life-Sustaining Treatments. 2. A brief educational intervention for physicians at the hospital. 3. Publication of an updated hospital protocol for decisions on limitations of Life-Sustaining Treatments. We analysed 100 randomly selected documentations of limitation of Life-Sustaining Treatments in adult patients before the intervention, and 98 after the intervention. Adherence to individual mandatory criteria and overall adherence to the regulatory requirements was evaluated.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Overall adherence to all documentation regulations increased from 1% to 63% (p < 0.01). Grounds for the decision were well documented both pre- and post-intervention (99% and 97%, p > 0.99). All other individual criteria improved: consultation with another licenced caregiver (65-89%, p < 0.01), dialogue with the patient or motivation why not (24-89%, p < 0.01), information to the family or motivation why not (23-74%, p < 0.01), the view of the patient (14-86%, p < 0.01) and the view of the family (4-70%, p < 0.01).

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: A moderate intervention in terms of cost and work effort for the organisation can significantly improve adherence to regulations regarding documentation of limitations of Life-Sustaining Treatments, although further improvement is needed.

articles.title: Analgesia Administration in Severely Injured Pediatric Trauma Patients: A Comparison of General and Pediatric Emergency Departments.
articles.journal_full: Journal of emergencies, trauma, and shock

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: The purpose of the study is to compare analgesia and sedation administration among pediatric major trauma patients managed in the pediatric emergency department (PED) versus the general emergency department (GED).

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This retrospective cohort study included pediatric trauma patients (<16 years) with an injury severity score (ISS) >15 treated at a single trauma center. Between 2013 and 2015, patients were managed primarily by surgeons in the GED; between 2019 and 2023, by pediatric emergency medicine physicians in the PED, following a 3-year transition period. Data on demographics, injury characteristics, pain assessment, and analgesia/sedation were extracted from the trauma registry and medical records. The primary outcome was analgesia administration rate. Secondary analyses compared provider type and analgesia rates between pediatric and adult trauma patients treated in the GED.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Seventy-three pediatric patients met inclusion criteria (GED: 36; PED: 37). ISS scores were similar (GED: 16 [interquartile range (IQR) 16-19.5] vs. PED: 17 [IQR 16-21], P = 0.16). Analgesia was administered to 48.6% of PED patients versus 33.3% in the GED (P = 0.18). Opioid use was 19% versus 13.8%, and sedative use was 21.6% versus 8.3%, respectively. Pain score documentation was more consistent in the PED. Children treated in the GED received significantly less analgesia than adults with similar ISS scores treated in the same department (33.3% vs. 78.3%, P < 0.0001).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Analgesia administration in severely injured children remained low across both emergency settings. While trends suggested improved management in the PED, findings may reflect broader changes in care over time, highlighting the ongoing need for standardized pain assessment and treatment protocols in pediatric trauma care.

articles.title: A Diagnostic Dilemma: Urosepsis Mimicking ST-elevation Myocardial Infarction: A Case Report and Review of the Literature.
articles.journal_full: Heart views : the official journal of the Gulf Heart Association

abstract.text: Acute coronary syndrome (ACS) remains a leading global cause of morbidity and mortality. Healthcare systems worldwide have established national guidelines to facilitate the timely identification and transfer of patients with ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) to centers capable of performing primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). Typically, ST-segment elevation (STE) on an electrocardiogram (ECG) is indicative of STEMI, prompting early intervention. However, rare cases of STE have been documented in the setting of sepsis or septic shock, with subsequent coronary angiography or imaging revealing normal coronary arteries. There is limited information regarding the exact mechanisms responsible for STE in the context of sepsis. We report the case of a 79-year-old Indian female who presented with epigastric pain and vomiting. Her initial ECG showed STE in leads I, aVL, and V2, accompanied by markedly elevated cardiac biomarkers. In accordance with the national STEMI network protocol, she received prehospital dual antiplatelet therapy and intravenous heparin before hospital arrival and was transferred directly for primary PCI. She was initially managed as a case of ACS; however, coronary angiography demonstrated normal coronary arteries. Further evaluation led to the diagnosis of septic shock secondary to extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL)-producing Escherichia coli urosepsis, requiring mechanical ventilation, four concurrent vasopressors, and continuous venovenous hemodiafiltration, with complete clinical recovery. Notably, her ECG abnormalities resolved within 72 h following prompt management of the septic shock. While STEMI remains the most common cause of STE on ECG, sepsis and septic shock are rare but important differential diagnoses. The underlying pathophysiology may involve inflammatory myocardial injury, transient coronary vasospasm, or global hypoperfusion. This case highlights the critical importance of recognizing septic shock as a potentially life-threatening STEMI mimic, to avoid unnecessary invasive interventions and to guide appropriate, targeted management.

articles.title: Recommendation on "Planned Out-of-Hospital Childbirth": the Position of the Austrian Society of Gynecology and Obstetrics (OEGGG).

abstract.text: The debate regarding the role of out-of-hospital childbirth (home births) remains controversial in many countries, including Austria; consequently, the Executive Board of the OEGGG, acting on behalf of our professional society, has decided to issue an updated recommendation concerning planned out-of-hospital births. This recommendation aims to articulate our position within the context of the forensic and clinical requirements of modern obstetric care and to support a revision of legislation governing out-of-hospital childbirth. It was unanimously approved by the entire OEGGG Executive Board following constructive discussion. We consider out-of-hospital childbirth (home birth) to be untenable, as it contravenes established obstetric quality standards-thereby violating the forensic rights of mothers and, even more significantly, the clear safety interests of the child (as a legal entity) during the birth process. Virtually all established clinical diagnostic and treatment methods cannot be employed in a home birth setting and are thus deliberately withheld from the child. Citing proven risks, the OEGGG opposes home birth and-like other professional societies-classifies it as unsafe. Given the elevated risks involved, our primary duty of care is directed toward the child during the birth process.

articles.title: Investigation of the knowledge of safeguarding in sports among medical and paramedical professionals in Rugby Africa, at Mauritius 7s 2024.
articles.journal_full: South African journal of sports medicine

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Safeguarding in sports has emerged as a critical issue globally, particularly for elite athletes in high-risk environments. Despite the presence of operationalised policy frameworks for safeguarding athletes from injury, violence, or harm, limited evidence exists on how well frontline medical professionals in Africa implement these practices. This study, therefore, investigates the extent of safeguarding knowledge, the degree of professional readiness, and the barriers to reporting among medical and paramedical personnel across Rugby Africa.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A cross-sectional study was conducted at the 2024 Rugby Africa Men's 7s in Mauritius. This study involved 19 Immediate Care in Rugby Level 2-certified medical and paramedical professionals from 11 African countries. Data were collected using a modified version of the Safeguarding Officer Pulse Survey, incorporating both quantitative and qualitative items. Descriptive statistics and thematic analysis were applied to assess knowledge, confidence, procedural awareness, and perceived organisational support regarding safeguarding responsibilities.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Over half (53%) of the respondents reported familiarity with safeguarding policies, yet only a small proportion (21%) had received formal training on how to apply those policies in practice. Confidence in identifying abuse was fair (63%), but awareness of designated safeguarding officers and reporting procedures was low. Environmental factors such as fear of retaliation (69%) and cultural silence (68%) were major barriers to effective reporting of safeguarding. Participants identified themselves (89%) as key protectors of athlete welfare, but lacked procedural clarity. Gaps in organisational education, policy implementation, and surveillance measures suggest systemic weaknesses in safeguarding infrastructure across Rugby Africa medical teams.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Enhancing safeguarding awareness, procedural training, and cultural shifts are essential for creating a safe sporting environment for African Rugby. Structured education and transparent reporting frameworks are recommended for similar tournament contexts. Additional multi-country research is necessary to guide broader policy decisions.

articles.title: The prevalence of Brugada syndrome in patients presenting to an emergency room in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Brugada syndrome (BrS) is a rare inherited arrhythmia associated with an increased risk of sudden cardiac death. Significant variation in the prevalence of BrS across different countries has been well documented. However, no study has examined the prevalence of BrS in Saudi Arabia. Therefore, our aim was to assess the prevalence of BrS in patients presenting to an emergency department (ED) in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This retrospective study included consecutive adult patients who presented to the ED at King Khalid University Hospital (KKUH) and underwent an electrocardiogram (ECG). Demographic and clinical variables were collected from the records, and ECGs were examined for the presence of a Brugada pattern (BrP). BrS was diagnosed when a type 1 BrP was observed with no secondary causes, and BrP was diagnosed when a non-type 1 pattern was observed. A prespecified sensitivity analysis was conducted, excluding patients whose presentation was potentially compatible with BrS (syncope, presyncope, cardiac arrest, and palpitations).

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: We included 1,000 patients. Men constituted 498 patients (49.8%). The majority were Saudi nationals (830, 85.6%) and the overall median age was 46 years (IQR: 30-65 years). The majority of the patients were afebrile at presentation (915, 93%) and a small number of patients took Brugada-inducing medications (27, 2.7%). The prevalence of BrS was 2/1,000 (0.002; 95% CI: 0.0002-0.007) and the prevalence of BrP was 26/1,000 (0.026; 95% CI: 0.0179-0.0390). Among the patients with BrP, 11 exhibited a type 2 pattern (42.3%) and 15 exhibited a type 3 pattern (57.7%). The sensitivity analysis revealed a prevalence of BrS of 2/912 (0.002; 95% CI: 0.0-0.0061) and a prevalence of BrP of 26/912 (0.028; 95% CI: 0.0178-0.0402).

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: This is the first Saudi Arabian study on BrS prevalence, suggesting a high prevalence and a notable proportion of non-type 1 Brugada electrocardiogram (ECG) patterns.

articles.title: Supraglottic airway versus endotracheal intubation in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

abstract.label: PURPOSE
abstract.text: Evidence comparing supraglottic airway with tracheal intubation in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest remains conflicting, and prior meta-analyses covered few randomized trials. We compared these strategies in adults.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched from inception to January 2026 for randomized and observational studies comparing the two strategies in adults. Primary outcomes were survival to hospital discharge and return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC); favorable neurological outcome was secondary. Risk of bias was assessed with ROBINS-I and RoB 2, and certainty with GRADE. Risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were pooled using restricted maximum likelihood random-effects models, with heterogeneity (I 2), subgroup, sensitivity, meta-regression, and exploratory trial sequential analyses.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Thirteen studies (246,659 patients) were included. Survival to hospital discharge did not differ between SGA and TI groups (RR 0.96; 95% CI 0.82-1.12; I 2 = 80%). Compared with tracheal intubation, supraglottic airway placement was associated with a lower rate of return of spontaneous circulation (RR 0.86; 95% CI 0.77-0.96; I 2 = 96%), particularly in the prehospital setting (RR 0.82; 95% CI 0.71-0.95). The direction of the association differed according to study design: SGA was associated with a lower rate of ROSC than TI in observational studies (RR 0.81; 95% CI 0.73-0.89), whereas SGA was associated with a higher rate of ROSC than TI in the two randomized trials (RR 1.09; 95% CI 1.03-1.16). Favorable neurological outcome did not differ overall (RR 0.99; 95% CI 0.88-1.11; I 2 = 61%), although the exploratory subgroup analysis showed a borderline statistically significantly lower rate of favorable neurological outcomes with SGA compared with TI among studies assessing outcomes at ≥1 month after the event (RR 0.90; 95% CI 0.81-0.99). Exploratory trial sequential analyses were overall inconclusive, with more supportive findings observed for ROSC. These exploratory analyses should be interpreted cautiously.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: In out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, survival to hospital discharge did not differ between strategies, whereas SGA placement, compared with TI, was associated with a lower likelihood of ROSC. In an exploratory subgroup analysis of studies reporting neurological outcomes at ≥1 month after OHCA, TI was associated with a higher likelihood of favorable neurological outcome compared with SGA. Given the mostly observational evidence, substantial heterogeneity, and reversal in randomized trials, these findings are hypothesis-generating and warrant randomized confirmation. Prospero Registration: CRD420261337076.

articles.title: Sex differences in management and outcomes after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest with angiographically confirmed obstructive coronary artery disease.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Previous studies have reported sex-based disparities in care, often disadvantaging women. Large registry analyses are limited by incomplete characterization of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest OHCA aetiology and coronary angiography (CAG) findings. We aimed to evaluate sex differences in management and outcomes among patients with angiographically confirmed obstructive coronary artery disease (CAD) following OHCA.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We performed a post hoc analysis of consecutive adult OHCA patients with angiographically confirmed obstructive CAD admitted between 2012 and 2023 using a prospective OHCA registry. Obstructive CAD was defined as ≥70% coronary stenosis identified by coronary angiography and considered the most likely cause of OHCA. The primary outcome of this analysis was 30-day survival. The secondary outcome was favourable neurological outcome at hospital discharge. Multivariable logistic regression was used to assess the independent association between sex and 30-day survival.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Among 1219 OHCA admissions, 634 (52%) patients had angiographically confirmed CAD, and 580 (91.5%) were included in the final analysis (median age 61 years, 15.3% women). ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction was the predominant aetiology in both groups (64% in women vs. 59.9% in men). Men more frequently had a history of CAD and prior myocardial infarction. No significant sex-related differences were observed in PCI utilization, procedural success, targeted temperature management, or extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation use. Thirty-day survival was 66.2% in women and 61.5% in men (log-rank p = 0.33), while favourable neurological outcome (Cerebral Performance Category 1-2) occurred in 55.1% and 53.8%, respectively (p = 0.82). Men more frequently exhibited multivessel CAD, whereas women more often had identifiable culprit lesions. In multivariable analysis, sex was not significantly associated with 30-day survival (adjusted OR 0.75, 95% CI 0.39-1.41, p = 0.37).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: In this cohort of patients with angiographically confirmed obstructive CAD following OHCA, no statistically significant sex-related differences were observed in management, procedural success, 30-day survival, or neurological outcomes. Men exhibited more extensive CAD.

articles.title: Validation and comparison of two prearrest prediction scores for in-hospital cardiac arrest survival.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: The optimal pre-arrest prediction model for survival with favorable neurological outcomes following in-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA) to aid Do-Not-Attempt-Cardiopulmonary-Resuscitation-decisions remains uncertain. This study aimed to externally validate the Prediction of Outcome for In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest (PIHCA) score and the Good Outcome Following Attempted Resuscitation (GO-FAR) 2 score and compare their performance for IHCA survival prediction.

abstract.label: METHOD
abstract.text: We collected data from IHCAs across three Swedish hospitals covering all care levels. We identified IHCAs through the Swedish Registry of Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation during 2015-2021 and extracted prediction model data through electronic medical records. Outcome measure was survival with favorable neurological survival defined as Cerebral Performance Category 1-2 at discharge, obtained from the registry. Prediction model performance was assessed with AUROC-curves (c-statistic), calibration coefficients and nonparametric calibration plots.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: We identified 647 IHCAs of which 501 were eligible for inclusion. Overall, 28% had survival with favorable neurological outcome. AUROC for the PIHCA score was 0.73 (95% CI: 0.67-0.78), compared to 0.70 (95% CI: 0.65-0.75) for the GO-FAR 2 score. The 95% CI for difference of AUROC-score when PIHCA score was compared to GO-FAR 2 score was -0.01 to 0.06, i.e. not significant. The PIHCA score calibration coefficient was 0.69 (95% CI 0.51-0.88) compared to the GO FAR 2 score calibration coefficient of 1.02 (95% CI 0.73-1.34). The calibration plots were adequate for both scores, although with some degree of miscalibration at certain ranges for each model.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: PIHCA score and the GO-FAR 2 score performed well and comparatively for prediction of survival with favorable neurological outcome following IHCA in a Swedish setting. Both scores could be considered for clinical use, in addition to sound clinical judgment, where the PIHCA score seems more adapted for clinical use.

articles.title: It takes two: development of simulation training for two-handed neonatal mask ventilation integrating a respiratory function monitor; a non-randomised before-and-after simulation study.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Facemask leak is common with a one-handed hold and can reduce the efficacy of neonatal resuscitation. Our objective was to assess a standardised, respiratory function monitor (RFM)-guided training intervention for two-handed neonatal positive pressure ventilation (PPV).

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Development of a two-handed PPV training algorithm occurred through an iterative process with learner and expert feedback. Participants performed PPV via a facemask on a term manikin with feedback from the RFM display (Monivent Neo100). We first piloted the training intervention on ten clinicians over six sessions. The intervention was then assessed through a before-and-after, non-randomised simulation-based study, blinded to the RFM, comparing mask leak, tidal volume and participant feedback. Mask hold style and hand preference were recorded.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Prior to the intervention, 17/40 (42%) had previously used two-handed PPV in clinical practice. Forty clinicians were included in the training study. Mask leak was significantly lower with a two-handed hold before training: one-handed median 27%, (IQR 3-73%) vs two-handed: 2.5% (1-31%), p < 0.01 median difference (95% CI) of -5.5 (-23 to -1). Post-training mask leak was comparable between holds: one-handed median 6% (IQR 2-55%); and two-handed 2% (0-5%), p < 0.01 median difference (95% CI) -4 (-18 to -1). Pre-training, 11/40 (27%) preferred two-handed compared with one-handed PPV. Following training 20/40 (50%) preferred two-handed.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Effective facemask ventilation in a neonatal manikin was associated with a two-handed hold without training or prior clinical experience. After training facemask leak was low with both holds. Feedback indicated increased participant preference for two-handed PPV after training.

articles.title: The safety of outpatient management for low-risk pulmonary embolism: A narrative review.

abstract.text: Acute venous thromboembolism (VTE) remains the third most common cause of cardiovascular death, following myocardial infarction and stroke. It represents a global health threat with a significant economic burden. Risk stratification for short-term adverse events is crucial for the management of acute pulmonary embolism (PE). Over the past decade, management of acute PE has evolved toward greater individualization, guided by risk stratification. Supported by the results of recent randomized clinical trials, American and European guidelines recommend considering outpatient therapy for patients with low-risk PE if adequate outpatient follow-up can be provided. Nevertheless, only a minority of them are currently treated as outpatients. In this manuscript, we examine risk stratification for acute PE and describe the main validated risk scores for low-risk PE, along with their limitations. In addition, we review several clinical trials comparing outpatient treatment with standard hospitalization. Furthermore, we address the barriers recognized by Emergency Department (ED) physicians that hinder the adoption of an outpatient management strategy. Additionally, we discuss the importance of implementing quality interventions and robust educational programs for ED physicians, as well as web-based point-of care tools, including electronic calculators of validated risk scores. We also emphasize key points for patient education and adequate follow-up to increase the rate of outpatient management.

articles.title: Prognostic utility of the revised post-cardiac arrest syndrome for therapeutic hypothermia score in pediatric patients with post-cardiac arrest syndrome.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: The accurate prognosis of post-cardiac arrest syndrome (PCAS) is critical for guiding intensive care and family communication. The revised post-Cardiac Arrest Syndrome for Therapeutic hypothermia (rCAST) score incorporates six readily available clinical variables and has shown promise in children. However, prior validations involved older children. We aimed to externally validate rCAST scores in a cohort of infants and young children.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We retrospectively examined patients with PCAS (with pre-arrest pediatric cerebral performance category scores of 1-3 and receiving targeted temperature management) admitted to a pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) between December 2016 and March 2024. Patients were stratified into low-, moderate-, and high-severity groups based on their rCAST scores. The primary outcome was neurological status at PICU discharge.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Among 5456 PICU admissions, 75 were included (median age, 17 months [interquartile range: 4-72]; 68% without pre-existing conditions). Favorable neurological outcomes occurred in 28% of patients overall, with 76% in the low (n = 17) and 73% in the moderate (n = 11) groups, but none in the high group (n = 47). The overall in-hospital mortality rate was 60%: 6% in the low group and 87% in the high group (P < 0.001). The rCAST score showed good discrimination for both unfavorable neurological outcome (area under the curve [AUC], 0.947; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.894-1.000) and mortality (AUC, 0.857; 95% CI, 0.750-0.964).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: The rCAST score demonstrated good discriminative ability for neurological outcomes in infants and young children with PCAS. However, unfavorable outcomes in some patients with low scores warrant caution in clinical decision-making.

articles.title: Diaphragmatic Rapid Shallow Breathing Index Versus Diaphragmatic Thickness Fraction for Predicting Weaning Success in Mechanically Ventilated Patients.

abstract.text: Introduction Timely liberation from mechanical ventilation is a central goal of critical care. This study aimed to compare two point-of-care ultrasound indices, the diaphragmatic rapid shallow breathing index (D-RSBI) and the diaphragmatic thickness fraction (DTF), in predicting successful weaning among mechanically ventilated adults. Methods In this prospective, single-center diagnostic-accuracy study, 44 adults who were mechanically ventilated for more than 48 hours but fewer than seven days and who met the readiness criteria for a spontaneous breathing trial (SBT) underwent diaphragm and lung ultrasound before the trial. Weaning outcomes were categorized using the Weaning according to a New Definition (WIND) framework; successful weaning (simple or difficult categories, n = 36) was the reference standard, whereas prolonged weaning (n = 8) was considered the adverse outcome. Diagnostic performance was assessed at operating thresholds and by receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis, and the two indices were compared using the DeLong test (SPSS Statistics v23 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY); MedCalc (Ostend, Belgium)). Results At a threshold of 1.2 breaths/min/mm, the D-RSBI showed strong diagnostic performance for successful weaning, with a sensitivity of 94.44% and specificity of 100% (area under the curve (AUC): 0.99, 95% confidence interval (CI): 0.97-1.00). The DTF discriminated poorly (sensitivity: 61.11%, specificity: 62.50%; AUC: 0.65, 95% CI: 0.42-0.88). The D-RSBI AUC was significantly higher than that of the DTF (DeLong p = 0.004). Notably, all eight patients with prolonged/failed weaning were also the eight most severely ill patients according to the Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation II score (APACHE II score, 13-21 vs. ≤ 10 in every patient who succeeded), and the direction of association for both indices was opposite to that reported in previous literature. Conclusions In this cohort, a D-RSBI ≥ 1.2 was strongly associated with successful weaning and outperformed the DTF. However, weaning outcome was completely determined by illness severity in this cohort, and the direction of the associations for both indices was inverted relative to prior studies. Therefore, these findings must be interpreted with caution and require validation in larger, multicenter cohorts.

articles.title: Traumatic High Cervical Spine Injury Presenting as Cardiac Arrest: A Case Report.

abstract.text: Traumatic high cervical spinal cord injury is a potentially devastating condition that may cause profound cardiovascular and respiratory instability through disruption of descending sympathetic pathways. In severe cases, autonomic dysfunction may contribute to marked hypotension, bradycardia, and cardiac arrest. We report the case of a 47-year-old man who sustained blunt trauma of incompletely characterized mechanism in a workplace accident and was found in cardiac arrest by a prehospital emergency medical team. Advanced life support was initiated, and return of spontaneous circulation was achieved after approximately eight minutes. The documented arrest rhythms included pulseless electrical activity and pulseless ventricular tachycardia. On admission, the patient remained intubated and mechanically ventilated and developed marked hypotension and bradycardia requiring norepinephrine support. Extended focused assessment with sonography for trauma showed no evidence of pneumothorax, pericardial effusion, or free intraperitoneal fluid. Computed tomography revealed a severe C2-C3 distraction injury with intersomatic avulsion, disruption of the posterior ligamentous complex, extensive traumatic hematoma involving the vertebral and spinal canal regions, and associated spinal cord injury. Following multidisciplinary assessment, the injuries were considered irreversible, with no feasible surgical or other outcome-modifying therapeutic option, and care was transitioned to comfort measures. The patient died approximately four and a half hours after admission. This case highlights the potential for severe high cervical spinal cord injury to present with profound autonomic cardiovascular instability and cardiac arrest and emphasizes the importance of considering occult cervical spinal trauma in cases of unexplained cardiorespiratory collapse following major trauma.

articles.title: Prognostic Impact of In-Hospital Emergency in Patients Admitted for Non-Surgical Intensive Care.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: We aimed to elucidate the prognostic impact of in-hospital emergencies among patients who require non-surgical intensive care.

abstract.label: METHODS AND RESULTS
abstract.text: In total, 4,483 patients requiring non-surgical intensive care from 2011 to 2021 were included. Patient backgrounds, in-hospital management, and prognoses were compared among 4 groups according to the hospitalization route: walk-ins (group A; n=636); ambulance (group B; n=2,748); helicopter/car-based emergency medical service (group C; n=565); and in-hospital emergencies (group D; n=534). The proportion of patients admitted to the intensive care unit after in-hospital emergencies was 38.0% among those with sepsis and 29.7% among those with other non-cardiovascular diseases. Furthermore, acute heart failure (AHF), sepsis and other non-cardiovascular disease were the most common diseases in patients with in-hospital emergencies (24.3%, 23.2% and 21.5%, respectively). Kaplan-Meier curve analysis revealed that the prognosis (365-day all-cause mortality) was significantly poorer in group D than in the other groups. A multivariable Cox regression model identified group D as an independent predictor of 365-day all-cause mortality (hazard ratio 1.227; 95% confidence interval 1.027-1.467) relative to out-of-hospital admissions, especially in AHF and non-cardiovascular disease.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Patients who required non-surgical intensive care after in-hospital emergencies mainly have AHF and non-cardiovascular etiologies such as sepsis. In-hospital emergency was identified as a significant factor associated with a higher 365-day mortality rate. A clinical approach to reduce their mortality is urgently needed.

articles.title: Delayed Cervical and Multifocal Spinal Metastases From Rectal Adenocarcinoma: A Case Report of Severe Canal Stenosis, Neurological Decline, and Septic Shock.

abstract.text: A 76-year-old male with a past medical history significant for rectal adenocarcinoma diagnosed in 2014 presented to the emergency department with worsening left arm pain, generalized weakness, and two syncopal episodes. The patient previously underwent sigmoid colectomy followed by low anterior resection and permanent colostomy. Imaging revealed diffuse spinal metastases with extensive epidural tumor causing multilevel severe canal stenosis and spinal cord compression. Additional findings included hepatic metastases, bilateral pleural effusions, supraclavicular nodal disease, and suspected leptomeningeal involvement. This case highlights the rare but devastating pattern of colorectal cancer metastasis to the spine and underscores the importance of early recognition of metastatic epidural disease, multidisciplinary management coordination, palliative care integration.

articles.title: Prehospital emergency response in a partial hand amputation with ulnar artery transection: a case report.
articles.journal_full: International journal of surgery case reports

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Approximately 50% of preventable trauma fatalities are associated with a lack of hemorrhage control and occur in the prehospital environment. The application and efficacy of traditional hemostatic techniques, such as tourniquets, gauze packing, and impregnated dressings, are frequently limited by factors including pain, risk of ischemia, wound configuration, and challenges associated with removal at definitive care.

abstract.label: CASE REPORT
abstract.text: We report the prehospital application of a hemostatic flowable biopolymer, Traumagel, in a 46-year-old male presenting with a partial hand amputation and complete transection of the ulnar artery. Following tourniquet application and initial hemostasis, Traumagel was deployed, permitting the safe release of the tourniquet, restoration of distal perfusion, and significant pain relief during a prolonged evacuation. The gel was removed in the operating room, and the arterial and metacarpal repairs were completed without complications or tissue loss.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION
abstract.text: This case exemplifies the seamless integration of hemostatic agents in conjunction with a tourniquet for the management of moderate-to-severe hemorrhage in a remote trauma environment. This prompt and comprehensive intervention for hemorrhage control in a remote location was crucial to an excellent patient outcome.

articles.title: Spiked Helmet Sign Associated With Acute Gastric Distension and Hemodynamic Instability: A Case Report.

abstract.text: The spiked helmet sign is an uncommon pseudo-ST-segment elevation pattern reported in critical illness and recognized by an upward baseline shift beginning before the QRS complex and a dome-and-spike contour. Its distinction from acute coronary occlusion is clinically important but can be difficult when myocardial injury, left ventricular hypertrophy, electrolyte abnormalities, or post-resuscitation changes coexist. We report a 34-year-old male with end-stage kidney disease on hemodialysis, hypertension, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and thrombotic microangiopathy who developed aspiration-related respiratory failure, peri-intubation asystolic cardiac arrest, septic shock, and marked gastric distension. During peak instability, an electrocardiogram showed sinus tachycardia at 135 beats/min, left ventricular hypertrophy with secondary repolarization abnormalities, and a spike-helmet morphology that was most prominent in lead II and less distinct in V3. Urgent nasogastric decompression evacuated gas and gastric contents. A repeat tracing obtained 20 minutes later showed a lower heart rate and partial attenuation of the dynamic morphology. A late tracing, obtained after resolution of gastric distension and hemodynamic stabilization, showed sinus rhythm at 83 beats/min and disappearance of the pre-QRS dome-and-spike configuration in lead II and V3, while baseline hypertrophy-related repolarization abnormalities persisted. The serial relationship supports a reversible extracardiac contribution, but incomplete serial biomarkers, echocardiographic assessment, intra-abdominal pressure measurements, and electrode-position documentation prevent definitive exclusion of concurrent myocardial injury or artifact. This case emphasizes integrating electrocardiographic morphology with bedside physiology, abdominal examination, imaging, and response to reversible interventions while continuing to evaluate for true myocardial ischemia.

articles.title: Lemierre Syndrome After Influenza A Virus Infection.

abstract.text: Lemierre syndrome is a rare condition characterized by septic thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein with metastatic septic emboli, most commonly affecting the lungs. We report a case of Lemierre syndrome temporally associated with influenza A infection in a previously healthy 21-year-old male. The patient initially presented to the emergency department with severe headache and tested positive for influenza A. Over the following seven days, his symptoms progressed to neck pain with decreased range of motion, hemoptysis, cough, and persistent myalgias. Despite four additional emergency department visits, his evolving neck symptoms were attributed to influenza-related myalgias and cervical strain. On the day of admission, examination demonstrated neck swelling, tenderness, restricted jaw opening, and pink foamy sputum. Laboratory studies were significant for severe thrombocytopenia, lactic acidosis, and sepsis. Imaging revealed right mastoid effusion, paranasal sinusitis, multifocal pneumonia, and a near-occlusive thrombus of the right internal jugular vein. Blood cultures grew beta-hemolytic group C Streptococcus and Peptoniphilus asaccharolyticus. The patient was treated with vancomycin, ceftriaxone, clindamycin, and metronidazole. Anticoagulation was initially deferred because of profound thrombocytopenia. Additional therapies included nebulized tranexamic acid, platelet transfusion, corticosteroids, and intravenous immunoglobulin for suspected immune-mediated thrombocytopenia. His hospital course was complicated by metabolic encephalopathy requiring intubation. The patient improved with treatment and was discharged after 17 days on oral antibiotics and rivaroxaban. He was subsequently readmitted 20 days later with a right empyema requiring bronchoscopy, chemical pleurodesis, and decortication. He has remained free of further hospitalization for one year. This case highlights the diagnostic challenges of Lemierre syndrome and the potential for diagnostic anchoring following an initially confirmed viral diagnosis. Although a causal relationship between influenza A infection and Lemierre syndrome cannot be established, clinicians should reassess the diagnosis when patients with confirmed influenza develop persistent or progressive focal symptoms, particularly neck pain or swelling, restricted jaw opening, respiratory symptoms, or systemic deterioration. Early recognition of Lemierre syndrome and prompt treatment are critical to reducing severe complications and morbidity.

articles.title: Locked (Overlapping) Pubic Symphysis, an Uncommon Pelvic Ring Injury, Following High-Energy Crush Trauma: A Case Report.

abstract.text: Complex polytrauma resulting from high-energy trauma may necessitate interdisciplinary care. A rare pelvic injury called locked (overlapping) pubic symphysis is commonly linked to unstable pelvic ring disruption and frequently necessitates surgery. A 25-year-old man sustained a high-energy crush injury after a large rock fell onto him. The patient presented to King Hussein Medical City Emergency Department on February 5, 2026. After initial assessment, imaging demonstrated a locked pubic symphysis with unstable pelvic ring disruption, a right sacral fracture extending into the neural foramina, lumbar compression fractures, left tibial and fibular shaft fractures, a left medial malleolus fracture, and retroperitoneal hematoma. Following initial resuscitation and stabilization, the patient underwent open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) of the anterior pelvic ring symphyseal locked fracture dislocation with symphyseal plate, and the sacral fracture was treated conservatively, in addition to intramedullary nailing of the left tibial shaft fracture and ORIF to the medial malleolus with screws. The lumbar spine fractures were managed conservatively. He was discharged after 11 days of programmed rehabilitation and physical therapy without any neurological deficits or unexpected events. This case highlights the importance of accurate imaging, meticulous preoperative planning, and multidisciplinary management in the treatment of locked pubic symphysis associated with complex polytrauma and the programmed rehabiliation. Early recognition, appropriate surgical intervention, and individualized conservative management of the posterior pelvic ring were associated with restoration of pelvic stability and a favorable clinical outcome in this case.

articles.title: Performance Indicators in Emergency Medical Services: A Scoping Review of Dashboard Applications in the Context of Crisis Management.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Emergency medical services (EMS) are critical for responding to crises and mass casualty incidents (MCIs). Rapid decision-making and effective patient flow management are essential for improving survival. Digital technologies-particularly dashboards-enable real-time monitoring of performance indicators and data-driven decision-making. This scoping review aimed to identify and classify key performance indicators (KPIs) used in EMS and to examine the role of dashboards in monitoring these indicators in both routine and crisis conditions.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A systematic search was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, Embase, and Web of Science from inception to January 2026, supplemented by gray literature. Two independent reviewers screened titles/abstracts and full texts. Data were extracted using a standardized form and synthesized narratively in accordance with PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews) guidelines.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Twenty-six studies were included. KPIs were categorized using the Donabedian model into structure (resources), process (response time, triage, coordination), and outcome (survival, satisfaction). Time-based indicators were most frequent. Eight studies (31%) reported dashboards, all in routine operations. Eight studies (31%) used real-time feedback devices (not classified as dashboards), and ten studies (38%) employed other digital tools. Only one study addressed crisis conditions, and it did not use a dashboard.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Dashboards are predominantly applied in routine EMS operations, with very limited evidence in crisis contexts. Developing crisis-specific, context-adaptive dashboards and standardized indicators should be prioritized to support decision-making and coordination in emergencies and disasters.

articles.title: Predictors of outcome in 215 patients requiring emergency department thoracotomy: A 2-year prospective study in a large urban trauma center.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Emergency department thoracotomy is a formidable procedure. We prospectively evaluated physiologic parameters in patients undergoing emergency department thoracotomy, mortality at the scene of the traumatic incident, and upon arrival, including cardiopulmonary resuscitation time, cardiovascular respiratory score, time to emergency department thoracotomy, and restoration of blood pressure, and identified predictors of outcomes.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This was a prospective 2-year study of patients in cardiopulmonary arrest requiring emergency department thoracotomy in a trauma center. Statistical analysis included univariate and stepwise logistic regression analysis.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Two hundred fifteen patients admitted in cardiopulmonary arrest required emergency department thoracotomy. Penetrating injury (n = 167, 78%), gunshot wounds (n = 142, 78.0%), stab wounds (n = 21, 12.6%), shotgun wounds (n = 4, 2.4%), and blunt (n = 48, 22%). The mean revised trauma score was -0.6, the mean injury severity score was -42, and the mean duration of cardiopulmonary resuscitation was 12 minutes. Emergency department deaths totaled 162 (75%), and 1-hour survivors totaled 53 (25%). Overall survivors were 6 of 215 (2.8%). Penetrating cardiac injury survivors were 6 of 74 (8.2%). Two groups were compared: (1) emergency department deaths versus 1-hour survivors-all physiologic parameters were predictive of outcomes (P < .0001) and (2) 1-hour survivors versus overall survivors-no physiologic parameters were predictive of outcome. Duration of cardiopulmonary resuscitation (P = .04), penetrating mechanism (P < .001), and exsanguination (P < .006) were significant. The cardiovascular respiratory score revealed a trend (P = .007). Death versus overall survival-restoration of blood pressure was predictive (P < .006). Stepwise logistic regression, using a 4-factor model, including no spontaneous ventilation, absence of pulse upon arrival, injury severity score >45, and blunt mechanism of injury, was 99.3% predictive of mortality.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: For patients presenting in arrest requiring emergency department thoracotomy, all parameters plus a cardiopulmonary resuscitation duration of 12 minutes are predictive of mortality. Seventy-five percent of patients can be excluded from emergency department thoracotomy. Emergency department thoracotomy should be applied selectively to patients sustaining penetrating cardiac injuries and some vascular injuries.

articles.title: Injuries to High School Football Players in Long Island, New York: A Five-Year Study.

abstract.text: Background American football has the highest injury rate of any U.S. high school sport, yet most studies examine a single injury type or position. We characterized injury patterns among high school football athletes in Long Island, New York, over five consecutive seasons, focusing on how injury patterns vary by level of play, setting, and position. Methods In this retrospective cohort study, certified athletic trainers and sports medicine physicians documented all in-season injuries among varsity and junior varsity (JV) athletes at 16 high schools from 2019 to 2023. Level of play, setting, mechanism, anatomic location, diagnosis, position, and time to return to play were recorded. Proportions were compared using two-sample Z-tests for independent proportions, with a two-sided p < 0.05 considered significant. Test statistics are reported as Z values alongside exact p-values. Results Among 3,861 athletes (2,093 varsity, 54.2%), 1,476 injuries were recorded. Varsity athletes accounted for a greater share of injuries than JV athletes (n = 1,104, 74.8% vs. n = 372, 25.2%; Z = 26.95, p < 0.001). Most injuries occurred in games despite far more practices (n = 732 of 1,308 injuries with setting recorded, 56.0%; Z = 6.10, p < 0.001). Direct contact was the leading mechanism (n = 796 of 1,344 injuries with the mechanism recorded, 59.2%). The lower extremity was most often injured (n = 672, 45.5%), followed by the upper extremity (n = 431, 29.2%) and head/neck (n = 187, 12.7%). Concussion was the most common specific diagnosis (n = 131, 8.9%). Profiles differed by position: offensive linemen had the highest proportion of concussions, and linebackers had the highest proportion of contact-related injuries. The proportion of athletes with a recorded concussion did not differ between varsity and JV athletes (Z = 0.53, p = 0.594). Conclusions A greater proportion of recorded injuries occurred among varsity athletes, in games, and through direct contact. Injury profiles differed by position, most notably a high proportion of concussions among offensive linemen. Because athlete exposure denominators were unavailable, these findings describe the distribution of recorded injuries rather than exposure-adjusted risk. These multiyear, position-specific data can inform targeted prevention and safety policy in high school football.

articles.title: The Nigerian Emergency Care System: Structural Challenges, Workforce Constraints, and Financing Gaps.

abstract.text: Emergency Medical Services (EMS) are a critical component of resilient health systems, enabling timely response to trauma, acute medical conditions, and obstetric emergencies. Despite Nigeria's substantial burden of preventable emergency-related morbidity and mortality, the development of a coherent and fully functional EMS system remains incomplete. Existing initiatives, including the National Emergency Medical Service and Ambulance System (NEMSAS), have demonstrated policy intent but continue to face persistent structural constraints. This narrative review synthesised peer-reviewed literature, national policy documents, and international agency reports to examine governance structures, workforce capacity, and financing mechanisms within Nigeria's emergency care system. Comparative analysis with selected high- and middle-income country EMS models was undertaken to identify contextually relevant system-level lessons. Findings indicate that EMS limitations in Nigeria reflect interdependent structural weaknesses rather than isolated operational failures. Governance fragmentation within a federal health system has hindered standardisation, coordination, and accountability, while workforce shortages, exacerbated by limited professionalisation and high rates of migration, restrict both prehospital capacity and clinical leadership. Financing remains inconsistent and heavily reliant on public budget allocations and out-of-pocket payments, limiting sustainability and equitable access. These domains interact in a reinforcing cycle that constrains system performance and the implementation of national reforms. Strengthening EMS in Nigeria will therefore require coordinated cross-domain reform that aligns governance authority, workforce professionalization, and sustainable financing within a unified national framework. Recognising emergency care as a public good and prioritising effective policy implementation are essential to improving health system resilience and advancing progress toward universal health coverage.

articles.title: Endoscopic Removal of an Intrabronchial Foreign Body Using Single-Use Flexible Bronchoscopy in an Older Adult: A Case Report and Review of the Literature.

abstract.text: Foreign body aspiration (FBA) is less common in adults than in children and occurs predominantly in older individuals with predisposing risk factors. Depending on the anatomical location of the foreign body within the tracheobronchial tree, it may cause life-threatening airway obstruction or lead to a wide range of clinical manifestations and complications, the occurrence of which largely depends on the duration of impaction. We report the case of a 74-year-old woman who was admitted with acute respiratory distress following the accidental aspiration of a solid food bolus. The initial choking episode resolved spontaneously but subsequently progressed to complete obstruction of the left main bronchus. The foreign body was successfully removed using a single-use flexible bronchoscope (Ambu® aScope 4 Broncho; Ambu A/S, Denmark) approximately one hour after emergency department admission and six hours after the patient's last meal. This case highlights the safety and effectiveness of flexible bronchoscopy for the emergency removal of tracheobronchial foreign bodies. It also underscores the clinical value of single-use flexible bronchoscopy when rigid bronchoscopy is unavailable, allowing prompt management while avoiding the need for interhospital transfer to a tertiary care center.

articles.title: National Football League Hand Injuries: Return to Sport and Performance.

abstract.text: Introduction Injuries sustained by professional athletes can severely impact seasonal performance and future abilities. The aim of this study was to characterize the impact of phalanx, thumb, metacarpal, and carpal injuries on the performance of athletes in the National Football League (NFL). Analyzing outcomes for football players is significant because the functional demands of each position vary widely. Methods NFL players who sustained phalanx, thumb, metacarpal, or carpal fractures from the 2012-2013 to 2022-2023 seasons were identified using the public database Pro Sports Transactions. Performance data were extracted from Pro Football Reference, including player position and the number of games missed, as well as the number of games played, games started, and snap counts in the seasons prior to and following injury. Players were excluded from the study if additional injuries were sustained at the time of the hand/wrist injury or if insufficient data were available to confirm the injury. Descriptive statistics were performed to characterize the cohort. Statistical significance was defined as p < 0.05 and assessed using a single-factor ANOVA. Results A total of 304 players sustained a phalanx, thumb, metacarpal, or carpal injury, with three players having injuries in two of these categories: metacarpal, n = 110 (35.8%); carpal, n = 80 (26.1%); thumb, n = 78 (25.4%); and phalangeal, n = 39 (12.7%). Linebackers (14.6%) and wide receivers (12.8%) were found to be most likely to suffer one of these injuries. Most occurred during the preseason or in September, near the start of the regular season (p < 0.001). The average number of games missed due to an injury was 5.5 games; by injury, carpal: 6.4, phalangeal: 5.8, thumb: 5.4, and metacarpal: 4.3 (p = 0.02). Sixty-five players were injured in their rookie season and 58 in their final season. These players were excluded from further performance analysis. The average change from games played in the preceding season to those in the following season was +1.0, with no significant difference when stratified by injury. The average change in games started was +0.5 games, with thumb injuries having the most significant impact, as games started increased by an average of 2.0 games (p = 0.08). The overall average change in snap counts was +72.8; by injury, phalangeal: +120.1, carpal: +31.5, thumb: +125.7, and metacarpal: +50.0. Safeties had the greatest decrease in games played, with an average of 0.8 fewer, as well as the greatest decrease in games started, with an average of 2.0 fewer starts after injury. Safeties also had the largest decline in snap counts, with an average of 94.9 fewer snaps after injury. Conclusions Phalanx, thumb, metacarpal, and carpal fractures are common injuries in NFL players, with an average of about 25 recorded per season, and they have a measurable impact on player performance. Players missed an average of more than 5 games due to these injuries, which is nearly a third of a normal season. Fifty-eight players did not return to the NFL, suggesting that hand injuries may be costly to both players and organizations and should be carefully managed by trainers and medical staff. However, there was an overall improvement in performance among the players who returned the following season, which varied greatly depending on the position of the player. This study should help guide team physicians in anticipating the impact on players after a hand injury based on their position.

articles.title: When Stroke Is Not a Stroke: A Case Report of Crimean-Congo Hemorrhagic Fever Presenting With Focal Neurological Deficits.

abstract.text: Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever (CCHF) is a potentially fatal tick-borne viral zoonosis with a wide geographic distribution, a significant case-fatality rate, and a risk of healthcare-associated transmission. Although CCHF commonly presents with nonspecific febrile illness followed by hemorrhagic manifestations, neurological symptoms may occur and can mimic acute stroke, creating diagnostic challenges in the emergency department. We report the case of a 72-year-old male farmer in the United Arab Emirates who presented with acute slurred speech, confusion, and right-sided facial droop, prompting stroke-code activation. Initial neuroimaging showed no acute intracranial hemorrhage, established infarction, or large-vessel occlusion. The patient subsequently developed worsening tachypnea, severe metabolic acidosis, thrombocytopenia, profound coagulopathy, mucocutaneous bleeding, acute kidney injury, and multiorgan failure. CCHF was confirmed by polymerase chain reaction testing. Despite maximal supportive care, including mechanical ventilation, vasopressor support, continuous renal replacement therapy, blood product transfusion, correction of coagulopathy, ribavirin therapy, and high-level isolation precautions, the patient developed refractory hemorrhagic shock and died later the same day. This case highlights CCHF as a rare but important stroke mimic. Emergency clinicians should consider CCHF in patients with acute neurological symptoms when accompanied by fever, bleeding manifestations, thrombocytopenia, coagulopathy, metabolic acidosis, renal dysfunction, shock, or relevant zoonotic exposure. Early epidemiological history, repeated clinical reassessment, prompt implementation of infection-control precautions, and multidisciplinary management are essential to reduce diagnostic delays and the risk of healthcare-associated transmission.

articles.title: Causes of Admission, Prescribing Patterns, and Outcomes Among Trauma Patients Visiting the Department of Trauma and Emergency at a Tertiary Care Hospital in Bihar, India: A Cross-Sectional Study.

abstract.text: Introduction Trauma is one of the most common, preventable causes of mortality globally. Its burden is rising, particularly in low- and middle-income nations, and hence, it is being acknowledged as an epidemic. The factors responsible for the high burden of trauma and trauma-related morbidity and mortality in resource-limited countries need to be identified and quantified. Additionally, there is a paucity of data from our setting on prescribing patterns among trauma victims. We, therefore, aimed to evaluate the burden, attributes, and outcomes of trauma as well as the prescribing patterns among trauma victims. Objectives The primary objective was to evaluate the burden, characteristics, and outcomes of trauma, whereas the secondary objective was to evaluate the prescribing patterns among trauma patients visiting the Department of Trauma and Emergency. Methods This was a hospital record-based, cross-sectional study conducted in the Department of Trauma and Emergency in collaboration with the Department of Pharmacology at Indira Gandhi Institute of Medical Sciences (IGIMS), Patna, which required a sample size of 369. The primary outcome was the prevalence of trauma, its characteristics, and death, presented as numbers with percentages, whereas the secondary outcome was the frequency of drugs prescribed from various classes. Results Out of 4,642 patients who visited the trauma and emergency department during the study, 1,137 were trauma patients. Thus, the prevalence of trauma in the study population was 24.49%. People aged between 20 and 40 years were the most affected (193, 52.30%), and most of the trauma victims were men (293, 79.40%). Rural people (284, 76.96%) were about four times more affected than urban ones (85, 23.04%). The street/highway was the most common place (124, 33.60%) for incidents, the time between 16:00 and 19:59 hours was the most common time of occurrence of incidents (93, 25.20%), and the ambulance was the most common mode of transportation (148, 40.11%) of trauma victims. Road traffic accidents were the most common cause of trauma, accounting for 152 (41.19%) of cases, while head injuries were the most common type of injury reported in 132 (35.77%) of cases. Analgesics, antibiotics, antiulcer and antiemetics, and intravenous fluids were major classes of drugs prescribed in 369 (100%), 369 (100%), 323 (87.53%), and 281 (76.19%) of cases, respectively. Out of 369 trauma patients under study, 28 (7.59%) cases died. Conclusion The prevalence of trauma among patients admitted to the trauma and emergency department was 20%. Road traffic accident was the most common cause of trauma, while head injury was the most common type of injury. Among the various classes of drugs, analgesics and antibiotics were the most consistently prescribed drugs. About 8% of trauma patients admitted to the trauma and emergency department died.
